en: In the *Cīvaravastu*, there is this summary verse (*piṇḍoddāna*):
Jīvaka, Bhāṅgaka, and likewise those with long fringes.
One should know that he was interrupted by the rains;
Upananda, being ill, met his end as his final act.
The summary verse (piṇḍoddāna):
Jīvaka, those with severed [limbs], three [types of robes], the rain-cloak (varṣāśāṭī), the sitting mat (niṣīdana),
itch, Sugata, silk (kauśeya), wool (ūrṇā), hemp (śāṇa), and linen (kṣauma).
The summary verse:
Khaṇḍa, Gopa, and Siṃha; likewise the journey to Vaiśālī; Celā, the anger of the Ṛṣis, and out of fear of Āmrapālī.
The merchant’s wife, the birth of Jīvaka, and the arrival of the physician;
Takṣaśilā, Bhadraṅkara, Udumbara, and Kārṣamāpaka.
The *rohitaka* tree, the royal garden, Mathurā, the wrestler’s wife,
the Yamunā, the path to Śiva, and Vaiśālī— these seven [are mentioned] regarding the eye and the centipede.
In Rājagṛha, five subjects are proclaimed as the section on Jīvaka.
In Videha, the King of Videha ruled his kingdom, which was prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and crowded with many people and inhabitants.
He had five hundred ministers, headed by Khaṇḍa.
The chief minister Khaṇḍa governed the kingdom with righteousness and adjudicated legal cases with justice, such that the entire body of citizens remained focused upon him.
He brought home a wife from a family of equal status,
and he sported with her.
He took his pleasure and enjoyed himself. While he was thus sporting, enjoying himself, and taking his pleasure, a son was born to him.
For twenty-one days—three times seven—as before, [the rites were performed] until the name Gopa was established for him.
Once again, while he was playing, enjoying himself, and diverting himself, a son was born to him.
As before, his name was established in detail as Siṃha.
Gopa and Siṃha gradually grew into young men.
The chief minister Khaṇḍa was already brave and valiant, having achieved mastery in the five branches of statecraft, by which he had become the foremost among ministers.
When he became powerful through his son, he remained there, surpassing all other ministers to an even greater degree.
Consequently, those ministers, their splendor eclipsed, consulted one another and, filled with resentment, went into the presence of the king.
Then, perceiving the opportunity, they said to the king,
"Your Majesty, who is the king?
The king replied:
"How can you have such a doubt, thinking 'I am the king; who else could it be?
They replied, "Your Majesty, Khaṇḍa is the king, not Your Majesty."
"If it should be his desire, he might depose the king from his kingdom, bind the royal turban upon himself, and exercise sovereignty, lordship, and dominion over the realm.
The king reflected:
"All these have been overcome by him; they are creating dissension because of him."
Then, at another time, while the king was seated surrounded by his assembly of ministers,
Khaṇḍa, the chief minister, entered the royal palace accompanied by hundreds of thousands of plaintiffs and defendants;
that royal palace became completely filled.
But when he had performed the royal duties and departed, that royal palace remained empty.
The king said,
"Sirs, this entire body of people is departing."
The ministers found an opportunity and said,
"Your Majesty has seen for yourself that which we now report."
"If Khaṇḍa should so desire, he could indeed depose him from the kingdom, bind the turban upon himself, and exercise the sovereignty, lordship, and dominion of the realm.
For kings are always suspicious of crows;
thus he reflected.
Thinking, "Surely it is as these people say," he became one who watched for an opportunity against him; such are the worlds of friends, enemies, and neutrals.
Then others informed Khaṇḍa:
"The king remains here, watching for an opportunity to seize you;
you should consider this."
Doubt arose within him,
and he began to reflect:
"Where shall I go?"
"If I go to Śrāvastī, Śrāvastī is under the control of the king; there too, this very same disadvantage would exist.
Likewise, in Vārāṇasī, Rājagṛha, and Campā, because they are each under the control of a single ruler, this very same disadvantage would exist.
Vaiśālī is under the control of a collective assembly."
"What is intended by some is not intended by the twenty;
in any case, I am going to Vaiśālī.
He then dispatched a messenger to the Licchavis of Vaiśālī.
"I shall go to dwell in the shadow of your arms," he said.
With feelings of deep respect, they gave him this reply:
"This very Vaiśālī is yours; welcome!"
Then Khaṇḍa, the chief minister, summoned his kinsmen and said:
"Sirs, I am setting out for Vaiśālī; those among you who wish to remain here may stay, while those who do not wish to remain should prepare, for we are departing."
The cowherds and the keepers of livestock were addressed:
"Drive the cows and buffaloes toward Vaiśālī.
The attendants were also addressed.
"Prepare yourselves! We are going to Vaiśālī.
Having thus urged the multitude of people, he went into the presence of the king, prostrated at his feet, and said, "Your Majesty, there is something that must be done."
"I am going to the park; may you watch over me.
The king said, "So be it; go."
Having caused the park to be beautified, he loaded the essence of the goods onto carts, covered them above with hard and soft food, and set out.
The ministers heard that Khaṇḍa was fleeing.
They went very quickly to the presence of the king and said,
"Your Majesty, Khaṇḍa is fleeing!
The king said:
"Sirs, go and turn him back! They equipped a fourfold army and set out, saying, "Khaṇḍadeva is calling you; turn back!"
He said,
"Sirs, for a long time this has been your source of comfort:
'Oh, if only Khaṇḍa would die or flee!'"
"He has been captured by you with little difficulty.
Go; he is fleeing!
Out of regard for the king's feelings, they turned back, forming a continuous line of guards, and reported to the king.
"Your Majesty, the chief minister Khaṇḍa has fled.
The king said,
"This is not good," and remained silent.
Khaṇḍa also eventually arrived at Vaiśālī.
At that time, Vaiśālī was inhabited by three districts:
in the first district there were seven thousand gabled mansions with golden turrets; in the middle district...
On the lower terrace there are fourteen turrets made of silver, and on the uppermost terrace twenty-one turrets made of copper;
in these, humans dwell according to their respective status—
whether superior, middling, or inferior.
In Vaiśālī, a formal agreement was established by the community:
whichever girl is born into the first group is to be given to one from the first group alone, not to one from the middle group nor to one from the lower group.

That which is given for the middle [grade] is given for the first category, or for the middle, but not for the lower; that which is for the lower is given for all three categories. There is no failure to provide a maiden; she is not given away elsewhere.
The jewel among women of Vaiśālī is not given to anyone;
she is for the common use of the community as a whole.
However, considering Khaṇḍa to be a preeminent man, his house was assigned to him within the first ward.
Thereupon, he began to attend to each individual matter;
however, whenever the assembly gathered, even though he was summoned, he would not join them. He was then addressed by the people of Vaiśālī:
"Khaṇḍa, why do you not attend the assembly? He replied, "It is precisely because of attending that this disadvantage has arisen; I will not attend."
The people of Vaiśālī said,
"Khaṇḍa, what harm could there be in assembling here?
and so he began to assemble them.
He did not give them a portion. They said, "Khaṇḍa, give us a portion."
He said,
"I will not even give you my consent, because it was from that very consent that these calamities have arisen for me.
They said:
"Grant your consent;
what harm could there be in this?
He then assembled in the marketplace and gave his consent.
Formerly, whenever the Licchavis of Vaiśālī sent a letter to anyone, they would send it with harshness;
but when Khaṇḍa began to give his assent, they wrote with courtesy—
those to whom he was courteous.
The letter has been delivered. They converse with one another:
"Sirs, what is the reason that the Vaiśālī assembly formerly wrote harshly, but now writes with conciliation?"
Others say:
"There is a distinction;
Khaṇḍa, the chief minister of the King of Videha, has arrived here, and they conduct their affairs according to his counsel, which is why they now write with such courtesy."
Khaṇḍa established dwellings for both the cowherd and the lion.
While the lion was playing, sporting, and enjoying himself, a daughter was born to him. Having performed an extensive birth ceremony for her as well, they established the name "Celā" for her.

A fortune-teller, having seen her, prophesied: "She will give birth to a son who, having deprived his father of life, will himself bind on the royal turban and rule the kingdom. Furthermore, while he was playing, sporting, and enjoying himself, a daughter was born to him.
Having performed an extensive birth festival for her as well, the name Upacelā was established.
She too was prophesied by a fortune-teller, saying: "She will give birth to a son endowed with all the marks.
Gopa, fierce and powerful, was destroying the pleasure gardens of the Licchavis of Vaiśālī.
The park-keepers said:
"The Licchavis of Vaiśālī are fierce and powerful;
do not destroy their gardens."
Although he was being restrained, he did not desist.
The park-keepers informed Khaṇḍa:
"Your son is destroying the parks of the Licchavis of Vaiśālī."
"Restrain him!
The Licchavis are fierce and powerful; they might do him harm.
He was then summoned by him and addressed.
"My son, the Licchavis of Vaiśālī are fierce and powerful; do not destroy their gardens, lest they bring harm upon you.
He replied, "Father, they have gardens, but we have none."
He said,
"Son, I shall request the community for the sake of a pleasure grove."
He informed the community, "I have no park for my two sons;
it would be fitting for you to grant me favor by providing a park from yours.
They then gave them a dilapidated park.
There was a great śāla tree there;
one [brother] had a statue of the Blessed One made,
and the second established a monastery.
Likewise, it was recorded by the Elders in a Sūtra: "The Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Vaiśālī in the Gopasiṃha Śāla grove.
Gopa performed thousands of improper acts;
the Licchavis censured him, reviled him, and spoke against him.
Then Khaṇḍa was summoned and told:
"Son, go to such-and-such a market town; there, carry out the business operations under your own supervision.
Stay there, lest there be an uprising of the community."
Having gone there, he began to have his enterprises carried out under his own supervision.
Then, at another time, the commander-in-chief passed away in Vaiśālī;
they appointed Khaṇḍa, the chief minister, to the position of commander-in-chief.
Having also exercised the office of general righteously for some time, he passed away.
The assembly of Vaiśālī gathered together,
saying, "Whom shall we appoint as general?"
Thereupon, some said:
"The assembly was protected by the chief minister Khaṇḍa;
let us appoint his very son."
Others said, "His son Gopa is fierce and valiant;
if he were appointed to the generalship, he would certainly cause a schism in the community. But his brother Siṃha is gentle."
"He is pleasant to live with and is able to please the mind of the community.
If it is the community's wish, let us appoint him as the commander.
This was the desire of everyone.
Having gathered together, they went into the presence of the lion and said,
"O Lion, please accept the command of general.
He replied:
"My elder brother Gopa—appoint him as the commander-in-chief.
They replied, "Siṃha, the office of commander-in-chief is not hereditary in your family; whoever is approved by the community shall be the commander-in-chief."
"If it is not to your liking, we shall appoint another general.
He reflected:
"If the office of general departs from our family to go elsewhere, that would not be right."
"In every way, I accept," he said;
thus he resolved. He was then installed in the office of commander-in-chief by them with great honor.
Formerly, when the people of Vaiśālī sent a letter to someone, they would write: "The community, headed by Khaṇḍa, commands you.
When Siṃha became the general, then it was written: "The community, headed by Siṃha, commands you.
Later, at another time, when Gopa was supervising his own enterprises in a certain market town, a letter arrived for that market town.
Gopa opened and read it.
He said,
"Sirs, previously the Vaiśālaka assembly used to write, 'The assembly headed by Khaṇḍa commands.'"
Now they write: "The group, headed by Siṃha, commands.
[They ask: "Has our father passed away?
They reply: [He has.]
Having passed away,
he became filled with resentment and went to Vaiśālī, where he said: "Brother, is it right for you to hold the office of commander-in-chief while I, your elder, am still living?"
The lion reported to him exactly what had occurred.
Incensed by this, he reflected upon the Licchavis of Vaiśālī:
"I have been treated with disrespect by the people of Vaiśālī; I shall go to Rājagṛha."
He sent a messenger to King Bimbisāra, saying,
"I wish to dwell under the protection of the King's arm.
The King wrote back to him:
"Welcome! Come in. He then went to Rājagṛha.
Thereupon, King Bimbisāra appointed him as his chief minister.
Later, at another time, the chief queen of King Bimbisāra passed away;
he sat with his cheek resting on his hand, absorbed in anxious thought.
Gopa saw him and said,
"Your Majesty, for what reason have you been standing there lost in thought, resting your cheek upon your hand?
He replied:
"My chief queen has passed away; why do you not remain absorbed in grief? "Enough, Your Majesty, let this sorrow be abandoned.
My brother has two daughters, endowed with beauty and youth, who are truly worthy of Your Majesty."
Among them, one had been prophesied that she would give birth to a son who would kill his father, while the second was prophesied to give birth to a son endowed with the auspicious marks.
"Which of these shall I bring for the sake of Your Majesty?
[He replied: "The one prophesied to give birth to a son endowed with the auspicious marks."
Then Gopa sent a letter to Siṃha, saying:
"The chief queen of King Bimbisāra has passed away; send Upacelā here, and she shall become the chief queen. He sent a reply to him in return.
"Even if we must go far and beyond, you alone are the one we must consult;
for whatever has been done by you is the ultimate authority.
You yourself know how the formal agreement was made by the assembly: 'A daughter is not to be given in marriage anywhere else except to those of Vaiśālī.'"
"But you should come and stay in the garden; I will have her led out to the garden, and then you may take her and depart."
Then Gopa, having looked back at the king, mounted his chariot and set out for Vaiśālī;
arriving there by stages,
he halted in the park.
At that time, the gatekeeper of Vaiśālī had died and been reborn among non-human beings. He informed the people of Vaiśālī:
"I have been reborn among non-human beings; this is my yakṣa-abode."
"Have a bell made and hang it around his neck.
If any adversary or enemy of the people of Vaiśālī should come, I shall ring the bell as long as he is either captured or flees.

Having fashioned a yakṣa in his likeness and tied a bell around his neck, they installed him in the gateway chamber with the sound of dancing, singing, and instrumental music, and with offerings of oblations and garlands.
Gopa sent word to Siṃha:
"I am staying in the park; come out.
Looking toward the Vaiśālī assembly, he went home and said to Upacelā:
"You have been given to King Bimbisāra; go and adorn yourself, and then depart for the pleasure grove."
She began to adorn herself;
she was seen by Celayā,
who said:
"For what purpose do you adorn yourself?
"I have been given away.
"To whom?"
To King Bimbisāra, she said:
"I am the elder; how have you been given to me?"
"If it is so, you may adorn yourself. She began to adorn herself, and the bell started to ring.

"The assembly of Vaiśālī is in turmoil; our enemy has entered Vaiśālī! Thinking this, Siṃha became terrified and, taking Celā with him, departed very quickly. Gopa also became terrified, placed Celā upon his chariot, and set out.
He was seen by the people of Vaiśālī;
they began to fight with him.
He, being skilled in five [martial] arts, struck five hundred Licchavis in their vital organs.
He said, "Sirs, I have struck you five hundred times in your vital spots; I spare the rest of your lives, so turn back!
They replied, "Not even a single being among us has been killed; put on your armor!"
They cast off their armor;
five hundred fell to the ground and were deprived of life.
Then, perceiving him to be a man-rākṣasa, they fled in fear.
Having arrived at Vaiśālī, they began to consult together:
"Sirs, this enmity must be avenged upon the sons of Bimbisāra.
Let us prepare a written document, place it inside a casket, seal it with sealing wax, heat it, and set it aside."
Having done so, they established it accordingly.
Gopa also arrived at Rājagṛha in due course and said,
"Upacela is disembarking."
She said,
"Father, I am not Upacelā; I am Celā."
"Why did you not tell me?
She remained silent.
Then, distressed and dejected, he went into the presence of the king.
The king saw him and said,
"Welcome, Gopa!
You have arrived."
"I have come, O King;
Upacelā has been brought.
"She has been brought, O King, yet she has not been brought."
"What are you saying? Having said 'Upacelā,' Celā has been brought. Let her be brought; let us see."
She was ushered in;
the king saw her,
and she was exceedingly endowed with beauty and youth, captivating in the realm of women.
Upon seeing him, the king was immediately captivated and said,
"Sirs, for a son who causes his own father to be killed does so for the sake of the kingdom. If I shall have a son, as soon as he is born, I will perform the binding of the turban of state for him."
Then, having been married with that great gathering of splendor,
she was given the name Vaidehī because she had been brought from the region of Videha.
He played, took pleasure, and amused himself with her.
At another time, King Bimbisāra went out on a hunt,
and in a certain hermitage there lived a seer endowed with the five superknowledges.
When the deer, terrified by a succession of arrows, emerged from the hermitage of that seer, it was struck in its vital organ by the king’s arrow; thereupon,
the seer became enraged and said:
"O King Kali, even my fierce deer avoids the precincts of the hermitage;
yet you have slaughtered a deer that had come to you for refuge. And thus was the king rebuked by the seer.
The army arrived and said,
"Your Majesty, who is this that reviles us?
The king replied:
"I am here, sirs.
Your Majesty, what punishment is there for one who reviles the king?
"The punishment for him is death."
When he had thus been abandoned by me,
that seer began to be struck down;
while being struck down, he made a false vow.
"Since I have been made a victim to be executed by this King Kali despite being innocent,
may I be reborn in that very place where I might deprive him of his life.
He reflected further:
"These kings are well-guarded and well-protected;
if I were to take birth elsewhere, I might never again encounter such an opportunity.
Therefore, by this very vow, may my rebirth be in the womb of this very chief queen."
Having made a false vow, he was conceived in the womb of Celā;
on the very day he took rebirth, a rain of blood fell,
and a longing arose within Celā.
"Alas! Would that I might tear off the flesh from the back of the king again and again and eat it! This report was then presented to the king, who summoned the diviners and questioned them.
They said,
"Your Majesty, this is the power of that being who has entered the womb of the queen.
The king remained lost in thought.
"How may her pregnancy longing be dispelled?
Others of a virtuous disposition replied,
"Your Majesty, present to the Queen yourself a covering of cotton filled with meat."
Then the king wrapped himself in a mattress filled with flesh and offered it to Celā; she,
thinking it was "back-flesh," ate it,
and thus her pregnancy craving was appeased.
Once again, a longing arose within her:
"Oh, how I would like to drink the king's blood!
This too was reported to the king.
Then the king had five veins opened and gave her blood to drink;
thus her craving was appeased,
and after nine full months she gave birth.
A boy was born, handsome, beautiful to behold, and pleasing; on the very day he was born, a rain of blood fell. Again, the king summoned the fortune-tellers and questioned them, and they said:
"Your Majesty, as it is seen in the scriptures, it is certain that this boy, having deprived his father of life, will himself bind on the turban and rule the kingdom.
The king reflected:
"In every way, for the sake of the kingdom, he intends to deprive me of my life."
"I shall give the kingdom to him myself;
for what reason would he deprive me of life?
At that time, Mahānāma the Licchavi was living in Vaiśālī.
In his garden there was a mango grove,
and in that very place, a plantain trunk suddenly sprang up;
it was seen by the park-keeper.
Immediately thereafter, it blossomed.
Filled with wonder, he informed Mahānāman,
who summoned the fortune-tellers and questioned them.
They said,
"Your Majesty, please wait;
on the seventh day it will burst open."
"From among them, a girl shall be born.
Upon hearing this, the householder Mahānāma was filled with even greater wonder; he stationed guards all around that grove and began counting the days.
Then, on the seventh day, when that grove had been cleared of stones, pebbles, and gravel, and sprinkled with sandalwood water—

Surrounded by friends, relatives, and kinsmen, accompanied by his harem, and attended by a great assembly of splendor, he went out with fragrant incense burners and bells set in place, draped with bundles of silk ribbons, strewn with flowers, and resounding with the music of many songs and instruments; while he was sporting, delighting, and enjoying himself in that garden, a plantain trunk burst open.
A daughter was born, beautiful, lovely to behold, pleasing, and endowed with all major and minor limbs;
she was then entrusted to Mahānāma’s chief queen,
who said:
"The name of this child shall be established.
Mahānāma said,
"This girl was obtained from the mango grove."
"Let her name be Āmrapālī.
Thus it was. When the householder Mahānāma had gone from the garden to his own home, the girl Āmrapālī was raised and nurtured; as before, she grew until she became a young woman.
Suitors came for her: the Krauñcas, the Śākyas, and other princes dwelling in various countries.
The sons of ministers, wealthy men, and guild-leaders.
Caravan leaders;
the householder Mahānāma reflected:
"I shall become an enemy to whoever I do not give [it] to;
however, a formal agreement has been made by the community.
Therefore, I shall first consult with the community."
He assembled the community of Vaiśālī and said, "Listen, sirs, brahmins and householders: a girl was born in my grove;
she was nursed, nourished, and raised by me."
"I shall give her in marriage to someone who is a worthy match for my own family lineage;
let the Gaṇas look on.
They replied:
"Householder, a formal agreement was previously made by the community: 'An unmarried girl, a jewel among women, is to be enjoyed by the community.
Therefore, let her be brought here for now;
we shall see what kind of girl she is."
She was led by him into the midst of the assembly;
seeing her, endowed with such beauty and youth, the entire assembly began to gaze at her from all sides with eyes wide with wonder, and said:
"Householder, this jewel of a woman is for the enjoyment of the community; she must not be given to anyone."
Then the householder Mahānāma, dejected in mind, went to his own home;
resting his cheek upon his hand, he remained lost in thought.
He was seen by Āmrapālī and questioned.
"Father, why are you so preoccupied with anxiety?
Daughter, because you are a jewel among women, you have become the object of enjoyment for the [monastic] assembly;
thus, my heart's desire has not been fulfilled."
"Father, are you dependent on others?
"Daughter, the Gaṇa has already made an agreement that a jewel among women is for the enjoyment of the Gaṇa;
and since you are a jewel among women, I am not her master."
She said,
"I shall become one who is to be enjoyed by the community if the community grants me five boons."
He gives a house in the first courtyard;
when one has entered, a second does not enter,
and he who enters takes five hundred kārṣāpaṇas.
"When there is a search of houses, my house will be inspected on the seventh day;
however, the entry and exit of those entering my house shall not be investigated.
Thus did Mahānāma convey Āmrapālī’s message to the group.
The assembly said, "So be it.
As for what he says— that she is a householder in the first *skandha*—
this jewel among women truly deserves to be a householder in the first *skandha*.
That which one says— namely, that when one person has entered, a second should not enter—
is also reasonable;
for this is the most detested of all enmities, namely, enmity toward women.
If a second person enters when one has already entered, they will certainly come to blows with one another.
As for what he says— that whoever enters must enter having taken five hundred kārṣāpaṇas—
that too is reasonable.
She certainly must have need for clothing and ornaments;
as for her saying that the inspection of the house should be made on the seventh day, that too is reasonable.
Whether it be done earlier or later, what contradiction is there in this?
What he says—that one should not inquire whether men are entering or leaving—is also logical;
for she is a courtesan.
If the entry or exit of men were scrutinized, who would enter her house?
Then the Gaṇa granted her five boons;
she became one to be enjoyed by the Gaṇa.
The Licchavis of Vaiśālī began to enter her house and to take pleasure with her.
In that regard, for some, passion departs at the mere sight [of her] because of their intense lust; for others, it departs at the mere touch;
and someone performs a manly deed with her.
She reflected:
"These are not men;
a strategic plan must be devised."
She summoned painters residing in various countries and said to them, "Gentlemen,
let each one paint upon the wall the likeness of whatever king, royal official, wealthy man, guild-leader, merchant, or caravan leader he has seen. They painted them exactly as they had been seen.
Then Āmrapālī, adorned with various ornaments, inspected the painted work and asked,
"Sirs, which one is this?
"This is King Pradyota."
Who is this other? King Prasenajit of Kośala. Who is this other?
Udayana is the King of Vatsa;
who is this other?
King Śreṇya Bimbisāra of Magadha.
Thus, when all had been questioned by her and everything had been related by them all,
she then examined everyone and fixed her gaze upon Bimbisāra.
She reflected:
"Of what stature and girth this man is, he will be able to enjoy himself with me.
Later, at another time, King Śreṇya Bimbisāra of Magadha, having ascended to the upper terrace of his palace, sat surrounded by a host of ministers and engaged in pleasant conversation:
"Sirs, by whom has such a courtesan been seen?"
The cowherd said, "Your Majesty, let others wait for now.
In Vaiśālī there is a courtesan named Āmrapālī, who is exceedingly endowed with beauty and youth, skilled in the sixty-four arts, and fit to be enjoyed by Your Majesty alone."
He said,
"Gopa, if that is so, let us go to Vaiśālī and enjoy ourselves with her.
He replied:
"O King, the Licchavis of Vaiśālī have long been your harassers, adversaries, and enemies;
they might cause you harm.
The king said:
"Indeed, men possess human courage;
let us go.
He said:
"If Your Majesty insists, we shall go.
Having mounted his chariot, he set out for Vaiśālī together with Gopa, and in due course, he arrived at Vaiśālī;
Gopa remained in the park.
The king entered Āmrapālī’s house;
then the bell began to ring.
The people of Vaiśālī were agitated,
saying, "Sirs, some enemy of ours has entered;
the bell is ringing!"
A loud noise, a great clamor, arose. King Bimbisāra asked Āmrapālī, "Noble lady, what is this? "Your Majesty, the house is being searched."
"For whose sake?
You must act for the sake of the King.
Why do you flee?"
"Your Majesty, do not be anxious.
On the seventh day, an inspection of my house will take place.
For seven days, therefore, play, enjoy yourself, and amuse yourself; after the lapse of seven days, I shall know the proper time."
He played, dallied, and enjoyed himself with her until Āmrapālī became pregnant.
Then she informed Bimbisāra:
"Your Majesty, I have become pregnant."
He gave her a ring and a finger-seal, and said:
"If it is a girl, she shall be yours alone."
Then, having dressed the boy in this tunic and tied the signet ring around his neck, you shall send him into my presence.
Having departed, he mounted the chariot together with Gopa and set out;
Ghaṇṭā remained silent.
They said:
"Gentlemen, Amitraka has gone out; let us search for him.
Five hundred Licchavis, having bound on their leather finger-guards and arm-guards, followed closely behind King Bimbisāra. Gopa saw them.
He said,
"Your Majesty, the Licchavis of Vaiśālī have arrived;
why does Your Majesty wish to fight with them?"
"Or are you driving the chariot?
He replied, "I am exhausted; I am driving the chariot."
"Fight with these very men yourself!
He began to fight with them,
and was recognized by the people of Vaiśālī.
They said, "Sirs, this is that very same man-rākṣasa; let us turn back.
Having turned back, they went to Vaiśālī and, having assembled, made a new pact.
"Sirs, this enmity must also be avenged by us upon the sons of Bimbisāra.
Then, after the lapse of nine months, Āmrapālī gave birth;
a boy was born.
He became handsome, beautiful to behold, pleasing, and so forth; he grew up to be well-bred and noble.
While playing with the Licchavi youths of Vaiśālī, he was addressed unpleasantly by them:
"Sirs, who is the father of this son of a slave-girl?"
"This one has been born from many hundreds of thousands [of past lives]. Weeping, he approached his mother, who said to him, "Son, for what reason do you weep?"
He related everything in detail.
She said, "Son, if they ask again, you should say: 'My father was such a man that he did not possess even one [virtue] that any one of you possesses.'"
If they ask,
"Which one?
they should be told, "King Bimbisāra."
When he began to play with them once again, they spoke to him in the same manner as before.
He said,
"My father is such that even one like him does not exist among you."
"Which one?
"King Bimbisāra.
They then began to beat him even more severely.
"Gentlemen, he whose enemy we are is his father.
As he wept, he related what had occurred to his mother.
She reflected:
The Licchavis of Vaiśālī are fierce and powerful;
it is possible that they will have him executed.
While she was thus absorbed in thought,
a large number of merchants set out for Rājagṛha taking their merchandise with them. She perceived them and said to them, "Seal your goods with this finger-ring and go."
"You shall go free of toll.
Take this boy to Rājagṛha;
having tied this signet ring around his neck, you shall station him at the gate of the royal palace."
They promised,
"So be it.
The son, having given a pearl necklace, was also addressed.
"My son, when you have sat down before the king as he presides over the court of justice, you must place a pearl necklace at his feet, mount him, and sit upon his lap.
If anyone says, 'This boy is not afraid,' you should reply:"
There was a certain son who was afraid of his father. He traveled by stages to Rājagṛha together with some merchants.
Having bathed him and adorned him with a signet ring, they placed him at the king's gate.
He approached the king;
having approached, he placed a pearl necklace at his feet and sat down upon his lap.
The king said:
"Gentlemen, this boy is not afraid.
He replied,
"Father, is there any son who is afraid of his father?"
Then, because the king addressed him with the word "fearless," the prince became known by the name Abhaya, Prince Abhaya. King Bimbisāra was exceedingly devoted to the wives of others.

Mounted upon the neck of an elephant, he entered the streets of the city; with eyes wide with wonder, he wandered about. At that time, in Rājagṛha, there was a certain merchant who was wealthy, possessed of great riches, and of vast enjoyments.
He brought a wife from a family of equal status;
as before, he enjoyed her company.
At another time, he addressed his wife.
"Noble lady, I am going to another country taking my merchandise.
She said, "Noble son, do so.
Taking his merchandise, he departed for another country.
Her garments were disarrayed and she began to be tormented by her afflictions.
King Bimbisāra, mounted upon the back of an elephant, was passing near her house.
Standing at the window, she threw a garland of flowers toward the king.
Then she was seen by the king and addressed:
"Come here.
She replied:
"O King, I am ashamed;
you yourself must enter.
Thereupon, the king entered.
He enjoyed himself with her;
at that time, she became beautiful, reached her season, and conceived a child.
She informed the king.
"Your Majesty, I have become pregnant.
Thereupon, the king gave her a finger-ring and a variegated fan, and said:
"If it is a boy, you shall send him to me after having him wrapped in this coarse woolen cloth and fastening a finger-ring around his neck;
if it is a girl, she shall remain yours. Thus he spoke.
The king departed.
Eventually, that caravan leader, having accomplished his purpose, arrived near Rājagṛha.
He sent word to his wife and others: "My dear lady, give rise to joy!"
"I have returned from my journey having accomplished my purpose;
it has been only a few days since I arrived."
Having heard what was said, she thought:
"I have committed such an improper act, and he has arrived;
how should I proceed in this matter?"
She reported this matter to the king,
and the king then gave her his command:
"Stay without fear."
"I shall act in such a way that he will not return quickly.
The king dispatched a messenger to him, saying:
"Caravan leader, I have need of such-and-such and such-and-such jewels."
"You must not enter here without him," he said;
for the sake of those jewels, he entered even further into the distance.
She, too, gave birth after the passing of nine months.
A boy was born;
he was handsome and pleasing to behold.
Women are untrained scholars.
Having placed her in a chest, filled it with clarified butter and honey, tied a signet ring around her neck, and covered it with a lattice-work screen, she commanded a female servant:

"Go, take this chest to the gate of the royal palace, prepare a mandala, light a lamp, and stand to one side until someone takes it. She did exactly as instructed. Meanwhile, the king was on the upper terrace of the palace, staying together with Prince Abhaya.
He saw a lamp at the gate of the royal palace;
thereupon he gave an order to his attendants:
"Look, sirs, why is this lamp burning at the gate of the royal palace?"
Having seen it, they reported:
"Your Majesty, a casket is standing here.
He said, "Bring it here."
And Prince Abhaya said,
"Your Majesty, you ought to give me whatever is in this chest.
The king recognized him and replied, "So be it."
When the king had the basket brought forward,
he said, "Open it!
It was opened, and there was a boy inside.
The king asked,
"Is he alive, or is he dead? They replied, "He is alive."
Then, having recognized the finger-ring and the comb, the king gave him to Prince Abhaya;
he was suckled, nourished, and raised by him.

Because he was addressed by the king with the words "Jīvaka" (the one who lives) and was supported by Prince Abhaya, the name Jīvaka Kumārabhr̥ta (Jīvaka, Nourished by the Prince) became established for him.
Then, at another time, Jīvaka Kumārabhṛta grew up and became a man.
He remained in the company of Abhaya.
Prince Ajātaśatru had been designated to the kingship while still unknown [to the public].
"We too shall learn some craft, so that it will serve as our livelihood in the future. While they were thus conversing,
the chariot-maker, dressed in white garments and surrounded by men dressed in white, entered the royal palace.
He was seen by Prince Abhaya, who asked other royal attendants, "Who is this?
and they replied, "He is a wheelwright.
[The prince asked,] "What does he receive?"
He observed their livelihood and thought to himself,
"I too shall learn the craft of a chariot-maker."
"I wish to see the king.
Having approached the king, he said,
"Your Majesty, I too wish to learn the craft of a chariot-maker."
The king said,
"Son, how will this be your livelihood?
[He replied,] "Father, a prince must learn all the arts."
"Son, if it is so, you must train yourself.
He began to train him in the craft of a chariot-maker.
Jīvaka also saw a physician, dressed in white garments and surrounded by men dressed in white garments, entering the royal palace.
He asked others as well, "Who is this?
and they replied,
"A physician."
What does he do?
He performs medical treatment;
if the patient lives, he receives a reward.
(MSV II 26) Then the preta, who was neither to be sought out nor questioned, reflected:
"I should study medicine."
He approached his father and said, "Your Majesty, please grant me permission; I wish to study medicine.
[The father replied,] "You are a prince; what would you do with the practice of medicine?"
"Your Majesty, a prince must learn all the arts.
My son, if that is so, then learn them.
He then began to study medicine.
He studied medicine,
yet he did not know the spell for releasing the skull-bearer.
He heard that in Takṣaśilā there was a king of physicians named Ātreya.
"He knows the spell for releasing the skull.
He approached the king and said,
"Your Majesty, I am going to Takṣaśilā."
For what purpose?
Therein was a king of physicians named Ātreya;
he knew the spell for releasing from the skull.
"I shall take her.
"Son, is this your livelihood? "Your Majesty, should one not study medicine?"
Alternatively, he should be trained;
my son, if it is so, then go.
He then sent a message to King Puṣkarasārin.
"This son of mine is going into the presence of Ātreya to study medicine; you must provide him with all necessary support.
Following this instruction, he arrived in Takṣaśilā in due course.
Puṣkarasārin had him read a letter and then introduced him to Ātreya.
"This prince has come into your presence; teach him medicine.
Ātreya gave him instruction.
Jīvaka, however, received it with particular distinction and practiced it more extensively than he was taught.
Whenever [the physician] went to visit Ātreya when he was ill, he would go taking one [student] with him;
on another occasion, he went taking Jīvaka along.
He prescribed medicine for the sick man, saying,
"Give him this and that," and having spoken thus, he departed.
Jīvaka reflected:
"This preceptor is exhausted;
if he takes this medicine..."
"He has consumed it and is dying this very day.
What was taught by the preceptor was not good;
a remedial measure must be devised."
Having gone out together with Ātreya, he entered again and said,
"The preceptor spoke thus."
"I have prescribed this medicine; it must not be given, but that and this should be given. They did exactly as they were told, and he was restored to health.
Then, on another day, he went again to the presence of Ātreya and asked,
"What is the news? [Ātreya replied,] "He has recovered."
Furthermore, this very thing must be given again:
was it that which was previously instructed, or was it that which was later? What was previously instructed by me, and what was later?
They said, "This was declared by them, this was personally instructed by you, and this was sent as a message by Jīvaka.
He reflected on this;
having realized that Jīvaka was wise, he said, "That which was instructed by Jīvaka must be given."
Affection arose in Jīvaka toward him;
wherever he went, he took Jīvaka with him.
Those other young brahmins said, "Preceptor, since you treat him as a prince, you must take great care of him."
"You are giving us instruction, yet you do not [do so for others]"—
he said, "Jīvaka is wise."
"I explain only a little according to my own ability, yet you do not divide [the teaching] in that way.
Because of this, they asked, "Preceptor, how is this known?"
"If I were to demonstrate this to you directly," [he said].

Thereupon, all those young men were sent to the marketplace with the instruction: "You must ask the price of such-and-such an item; you, of such-and-such an item"; and Jīvaka was also instructed: "You too must ask for such-and-such an item."
Those young brahmins carried out exactly as they had been instructed.
Having done what he was told, Jīvaka reflected:
"If the preceptor asks for the price of some other article, what should I say?"
"In every way, I shall ask for the price of all the goods.
Having been thus instructed, they all went into the presence of the preceptor and reported exactly as they had been told.
Then Ātreya began to ask for the price of the goods that had not been mentioned.
"Young man, what is the price of such-and-such an article?
He replied,
"I do not know."
Others were asked and said, "We do not know. Then Jīvaka was asked.
By him, the value of all goods was declared.
Ātreya said:
"Young men, have you heard?"
"I have heard this;
I speak for this purpose," [said Jīvaka]. "I am wise and explain only a little, while he distributes [the teaching] according to his own capacity.
Furthermore, I shall verify this through direct perception.
They were told by him, "Go to Mount Saralaka and bring back a medicine that is not a medicine. They went, and each took whatever non-medicine they desired. Jīvaka reflected:
"There is nothing that cannot be used as medicine. With this thought, he took some reed roots and a stone-powder.
On the way, Jīvaka saw a cowherd woman carrying a jar of curd and a lump of sour gruel, setting out toward the presence of Ātreya while suffering intensely from an eye disease.
She was asked by him,
"Where are you going? and she explained.
He instructed her on the medicinal treatment for that very condition; she carried it out,
and having immediately recovered, she became full of faith and said:
"This is your jar of curd and this is a lump of whey," she said.
He took the lump of whey, but the jar of curd was given back by her;
taking the lump of whey, he set out.
When those young brahmins saw an elephant's footprint on the road,
they began to examine it;
and Jīvaka arrived and said:
"What is this?
"An elephant's footprint. "This is not an elephant's footprint."
"This is the footprint of a female elephant;
she is blind in her right eye and will give birth to a young elephant this very day.
A woman was riding upon her."
She too was blind in her right eye,
pregnant, and would give birth to a son this very day.
When he had gone into the presence of Ātreya,
that which had been brought by him was presented to him;
Ātreya said:
"O young men, all this is medicine; first, for such-and-such a disease, it is taken with water according to this procedure; and so it is for other diseases as well. Thus was Jīvaka questioned.
"What have you brought?
He replied, "Preceptor, there is no medicine at all that is not medicine;
however, I have brought the root of a *śara* grass, a stone-powder, and a lump of *kiṭāla*."
What is the use of these?
For one stung by a scorpion, incense made from the roots of *śara* grass is administered;
a poultice made from a lump of *kiṭāla* is applied.
At that time, jars of curd were being broken by pebbles.
Ātreya sneezed.
The young students thought, "The teacher is angry with him."
They said, "Preceptor, is it only this?
On the way as we were coming, we saw an elephant's footprint.
He replied:
"This is the footprint of a female elephant;
she is blind in her right eye and is pregnant."
This very day she will give birth;
she will bring forth a young elephant,
mounted upon which is a woman of beautiful form.
She too was blind in her right eye,
pregnant,
and would give birth this very day.
"He will give birth to a son. Ātreya asked, "Is this true?
"It is true, Preceptor."
"How is this known—that this is the footprint of a male elephant and that is the footprint of a female elephant? He replied, "Preceptor, we were raised in the royal palace;
how could we not know?"
The footprint of a male elephant is circular, while that of a female elephant is elongated.
How is it known that she is blind in her right eye?
She has gone away moving with her left side.
How is it known that she is pregnant?
Because her two feet have gone numb.
How is it known that she will give birth this very day?
She passed urine mixed with semen.
How was it known that she would give birth to a colt?
She went along, repeatedly pressing down upon her right foot.
How was it known that a woman had mounted [the elephant] there? By the fact that, having dismounted, she urinated between its two forefeet.
How was it known that she too was blind in her right eye?
She went along gathering flowers with her left hand.
How was it known that she too was pregnant?
Because she walked while frequently pressing down on her heel.
"How is it known that she will give birth this very day?
"He has discharged semen and urine.
"Nevertheless, if the Preceptor has a doubt, that caravan is at such-and-such a place; send some young brahmin there."
He sent a young brahmin,
and everything was exactly as Jīvaka had described.
Ātreya addressed the young brahmins:
"Students, have you heard? "Preceptor, we have heard.
"Such is Jīvaka, wise."
Jīvaka had mastered everything except the spell for releasing from the skull-disease (*kapālamocanī*).
At that time, a certain man afflicted with the skull-disease went to Ātreya and said, "Ātreya, please treat me.
He replied:
"O man, for now dig a pit and bring some cow dung;
tomorrow I shall perform medical treatment for you.
This was overheard by Jīvaka.
He followed closely behind him and said,
"O man, whatever I have learned, I have learned it all for the sake of the welfare of sentient beings;
yet I have not learned the *kapālamocanī*."
"Therefore, place it now in a secure spot so that I may see your work being performed.
He replied,
"So be it."
He was placed by him in a hidden location;
then Ātreya arrived and buried that man in a pit,
and by means of the *kapālamocanī* spell, he released the skull.
He began to seize that living creature with a pair of tongs. Jīvaka said, "Teacher, do not act rashly!
This son of good family will pass away this very day."
He said,
"Jīvaka, have you come?
He replied.
"I have come from my preceptor.
Therefore, how is he to be caught by you? Preceptor, heat a pair of tongs and touch him on the back."
"He will contract his feet;
then you shall remove [the bowl].
He did exactly so.
Having recovered his health,
Ātreya said,
"Jīvaka, I am well-pleased; come after you have bathed, and I shall give you the *kapālamocanī* spell."
Having returned after bathing,
he gave him the *kapālamocanī* spell and said:
"Jīvaka, this is our livelihood; it must not be employed by you here in this kingdom.
"So be it, Preceptor," Jīvaka replied. Having taken leave of Ātreya, he went into the presence of King Puṣkarasārin and addressed him.
"I have studied medicine;
I am going.
Now at that time, the Khaṣas named Pāṇḍavas were in rebellion against King Puṣkarasārin.
He said, "Jīvaka, first subdue those Khaśas called the Pāṇḍavas; afterwards you may go.
In this way, our worldly affairs will be settled."
Because you are both wise and capable,
he promised him [the task]. Thereupon, having provided him with a fourfold army, he was dispatched.
By him those Pāṇḍavas and Khaṣas were subdued;
having taken captives, cattle, and taxes, he returned safely and presented them to the king exactly as they had been brought.
Being well-pleased, he gave his approval to that very act; he, in turn, gave it to Ātreya.
Then Jīvaka, proceeding by stages, arrived at the city of Bhadrankara and remained there for the rainy season retreat.
There he studied the treatise called *Sarvabhūtaruta*.
He set out from the city of Bhadraṃkara.
And a certain man, carrying a load of wood, was entering the city, his body reduced on all sides to nothing but bone and skin.
He was seen by Jīvaka, who said to him,
"O man, by what means has your condition become such as this?
He replied, "I too do not know."
"Moreover, this bundle of wood has been taken up by me;
such is my current condition," he thought,
for he was an expert in the examination of timber.
He said,
"O man, is this load of wood for sale?
"It is for sale."
"For what price?
"For five hundred kārṣāpaṇas. Thereupon, he was purchased by him.
Then, while he was searching, he saw a jewel named Sarvabhūtaprasādana.
Its power was such that when it was placed before a sick person, the disease was seen exactly as it was, like objects inside a house seen by means of a lamp.
He eventually reached Udumbarikā in due course.
In that place, there was a certain man who measured by the *āḍhaka*.
Having measured a *droṇa*, he struck it on the head with an *āḍhaka*.
Jīvaka saw him and said, "O man, why do you do this?"
"My head itches excessively;
come, let us look. He sat down and showed him his head.
Then Jīvaka placed upon his head a gem that inspires faith in all living beings, until he saw a centipede there.
He then said,
"O man, a centipede is sitting on your head!"
Falling at his feet, he said, "Please provide me with medical treatment. He [the physician] gave his promise. Jīvaka reflected:
"By the instruction of my preceptor alone, I shall perform his medical treatment.
He was told by him:
"O man, dig a pit today and bring a stone; I will perform the treatment."
Having prostrated at his feet, he departed.

On another day, Jīvaka also had that man buried in a pit; having released the skull with the *kapālamocanī* spell, he touched a centipede with a pair of tongs, and by it, the man's feet were contracted.
Then, having been seized with that pincers, he was cast out;
he recovered his health, and he gave him five hundred kārṣāpaṇas.
Therefore, they were sent to Ātreya.
Then Jīvaka arrived at Rohītaka.
In Rohītaka, there was a certain householder’s park, which was abundant in flowers, fruits, and water.
Having died while being excessively attached to that place, he was reborn among those very same non-human beings.
His son became the master of the house,
and he stationed a guard-man in that garden.
He was killed by that non-human being;
a second was stationed,
and he too was killed.
That householder’s son gave away that park.
Eventually, a certain man suffering from abdominal disease, who had been rejected by all physicians, went to that park and stayed there for the night.
"Alas! May a non-human being kill me!
And at that very moment, Jīvaka arrived there for the night's lodging;
just then, that non-human being began to rush toward the pregnant woman.
The disease of dropsy emerged and said,
"I seized this man previously; for what reason do you attack him?"
"There is no one who will give you the goat's bristle incense by which you might flee for twelve yojanas," he said.
The other replied,
"There is also no one who will give you radish seeds ground with whey, by which you would fall apart piece by piece."
Jīvaka heard everything. Rising early in the morning, he went to that householder and said,
"Householder, why have you abandoned this garden, which is so well-endowed with flowers, fruits, and water?"
The householder reported to him exactly what had occurred.
He said,
"Householder, offer incense made from the hair of a goat."
The non-human fled for twelve yojanas.
The householder offered incense made from goat's hair;
the non-human fled for twelve yojanas.
That householder also gave five hundred kārṣāpaṇas to Jīvaka;
he, in turn, sent them to Ātreya.
Then Jīvaka questioned the woman with the abdominal tumor.
"O man, for what purpose do you stand here in this garden inhabited by non-human beings?
He related to him exactly what had occurred.
Jīvaka said:
"Grind radish seeds with buttermilk and drink it;
you will become well.
He drank it.
He recovered his health. That man also gave five hundred kārṣāpaṇas to Jīvaka,
and he sent them as well to Ātreya.
Then Jīvaka, traveling by stages, arrived at Mathurā;
he rested at the foot of a tree outside Mathurā,
just as one wrestler had been defeated by another.
His intestines were turned inside out;
thinking he was dead, he was carried outside.
And on that tree sat a female lizard with her young.
She was addressed by those cubs:
"Mother, give us some meat.
She replied:
"Son, where is the meat? They replied, "Mother, this wrestler has been killed by another wrestler; he has passed away and is being carried away."
"Son, the King of Physicians, Jīvaka, has arrived here. It is possible that he will restore him to health.
"Mother, by what means does he become healthy?"
If his intestines were touched by these powders,
Jīvaka heard all of that;
thereupon he rose, went to the side of the dead man, and asked, "Sirs, what is this?"
They said,
"One wrestler has been struck down by another;
he has passed away."
Jīvaka said,
"Wait;
let me see."
They placed it there.
Then Jīvaka, having placed upon his head the jewel that inspires faith in all beings, examined it;
he saw that the intestines were in a state of disorder.
He placed the powder into a tube and blew it into the mouth with his breath;
the intestines were touched by the powder,
and he was restored to health.
He, in turn, gave five hundred kārṣāpaṇas to Jīvaka;
he sent them to Ātreya.
In Mathurā, there was a certain householder.
His wife was endowed with beauty and youth;
he died while being excessively attached to her,
and a worm appeared within that very womb.
Whomever she enjoyed with, he would die;
consequently, no one at all enjoyed her company.
She heard that the physician Jīvaka had arrived there.
She went into his presence and said,
"Jīvaka, I have an illness; provide me with medical treatment."
Having seen her and heard their conversation, Jīvaka became impassioned and said,
"I will provide medical treatment on the condition that you enjoy yourself with me.
She replied:
"I am ashamed.
He said,
"There is no other treatment for you."
"There is no love equal to that for oneself. She then made a vow; consequently, she stripped herself naked.
A piece of flesh was placed at the opening of the womb;
then that worm attached itself to it,
and he seized it and cast it out.
Having recovered her health, she, being obsessed with sensual desire, displayed a provocative sign.
He, covering his ears, said: "Sister, you are my [sister]."
"This was your medical treatment; it was done by me.
She gave him five hundred kārṣāpaṇas, which he then sent to Ātreya.
Then Jīvaka gradually reached the bank of the Yamunā. There he saw a human corpse; its heels and network of tendons were being pulled away by fish.
He opened and closed his eyes;
Jīvaka observed all of that, noting how the joints, ligaments, ankles, and other parts were situated exactly as they were in Sandhibandhā.
He proceeded by stages until he reached Vaiśālī;
there, a Malla struck another Malla with a blow of his palm, causing him to fall into a pit.
He then went into the presence of Jīvaka.
He pulled the network of sinews from that heel and inserted it;
for this, he was given five hundred kārṣāpaṇas,
which he gave to Abhaya’s mother.
In Vaiśālī, there was a certain man;
a centipede entered his ear and gave birth there.
Seven hundred children were born;
afflicted by earaches, he went to Jīvaka and said,
"Please provide medical treatment."
Jīvaka reflected:
"Previously I performed my work according to the instructions of my preceptor; now I shall perform it according to my own judgment.
He then addressed that man.
"Go, my good man, have a leaf-pavilion constructed;
having covered it with blue cloths, place a drum beneath it and heat the ground."
He carried out everything exactly as instructed.
Then Jīvaka had that man laid upon the ground and sprinkled the earth with water;
thereafter, the drum was struck.
Thinking it was the rainy season, the centipede went out.
Then Jīvaka placed a piece of flesh at the base of her ear;
she entered again, took up her offspring, and emerged.
Together with his children, he was sprinkled with a piece of meat;
then Jīvaka discarded that piece of meat,
and the man recovered his health.
He gave five hundred kārṣāpaṇas;
those too were given by him to Abhaya’s mother.
He then proceeded in due course to Rājagṛha.
King Bimbisāra heard that Jīvaka had arrived; he gave an order to Prince Ajātaśatru, saying, "Son, your brother is coming; go to meet him. He went out to meet him.
Jīvaka heard that Prince Ajātaśatru was coming out to meet him.
He reflected:
"If I accept his coming out to meet me, then when he becomes king, he will cause me harm."
He turned back and entered through another gate.
On another occasion, Jīvaka was walking along surrounded by a great multitude of people with his mind distracted;
at that moment, a certain brahmin afflicted with an eye disease approached Jīvaka.
"Prescribe a medicine for me," he said.
Enraged, the other replied,
"Fill it with ashes."
It was filled with that straight ash;
he recovered,
and another person’s eye disease was also cured.
He set out toward Jīvaka;
he was seen by that brahmin and asked:
"O man, where are you going?"
He explained it as it truly is,
and he said:
"What do you have to do with Jīvaka?"
"Do that which was instructed to me by him," he said;
and being full of faith,
he was blinded when his eyes were filled with those ashes.
At another time, a tumor developed on the head of King Bimbisāra.
He gave an order to his ministers:
"Sirs, let a physician be summoned."
Summoned by his ministers,
he was addressed by the king: "Sirs,
a tumor has grown upon my head."
"Perform medical treatment," they were told. They replied,
"Your Majesty, while the great physician Jīvaka is present, how shall we proceed?"
The king said, "Gentlemen, let Jīvaka be summoned.
They summoned him,
and the king said:
"Jīvaka, provide medical treatment. Jīvaka replied, "Your Majesty, I will do so on one condition: that I myself shall bathe Your Majesty."
"Do so.
Then Jīvaka, while giving the myrobalan fruit, administered digestive medicines;
he also prepared five hundred jars infused with digestive medicinal substances.
When it was ripe, it was secretly touched with a razor and burst open. Then healing substances were applied;
five hundred jars were infused with those healing substances.
That wound had healed, becoming even-skinned and even-haired. As soon as he had bathed, the king said,
"Jīvaka, perform a medical treatment."
He said,
"Your Majesty, please eat.
Thereupon, the king ate.
"Jīvaka, perform a medical treatment.
"Your Majesty, it has already been done.
At the end of that, he touched it with his hand.
He did not know in which part the wound was located;
he took a mirror and looked, yet even so he did not see it,
and he asked the queen.
She, too, did not know in which part the wound had been;
the king was struck with great wonder and said to his ministers,
"Confer upon you, Jīvaka, the inauguration as King of Physicians."
That blind man said,
"Your Majesty, is his consecration being performed out of affection for a son,
or rather because of the physician's skill?"
He said,
"Because of the physician's lack of skill;
if this is so, then I myself have been blinded by him."
Jīvaka said, "O man, I do not even perceive you; how then shall I restore you to health?
He replied:
"This is true; however, that to whom you gave instruction was instructed by me.
What was instructed?
So-and-so."
Jīvaka said:
"His element is one; yours is another."
"Now, do this and that;
you will recover.
He did so.
Having recovered his health,
he said:
"Your Majesty, let the consecration of this man as the King of Physicians be performed."
Mounted upon the back of an elephant and accompanied by a great assembly of splendor, he was consecrated into the sovereignty of physicians.
At that time, a certain householder in Rājagṛha was afflicted with a chronic abdominal disease (gulma) and was rejected by all the physicians.
He reflected:
"I shall go to Jīvaka.
If he performs the medical treatment, it will be excellent; if not, I shall take my own life."
He went into the presence of Jīvaka and said,
"Jīvaka, provide medical treatment for me.
He replied:
"O man, the medicines you require are difficult to obtain.
He reflected:
"I have been rejected even by Jīvaka."
Thinking, "What is the right course here? I shall kill myself," he went to the cemetery.
There, as the funeral pyre was blazing, a brown mongoose and a sandalwood iguana fell into it while fighting.
Afflicted by hunger, he ate them both;
then it rained,
and he drank the water from the funeral pyre flowing out from the cremation ground.
Not far from the cremation ground was a cow-pen;
having gone there, he ate kodrava rice and drank buttermilk,
and his abscess burst open.
Having been purged from above and below, he became as he was before. At a later time, a tumor arose in the private parts of Vaidehī;
she informed the king.
The king said to Jīvaka,
"Provide medical treatment for my stepmother. He gave his promise.
Then, having formed the rice balls into a lump, they were given by the nurse with the instruction,
"She should be made to sit near this. She was then made to sit by her.
When Jīvaka saw the lump of meat, he observed that it was in such-and-such a place;
thereupon, digestive substances were administered.
Knowing it was cooked, she placed a blade of grass inside a well-prepared ball of food and said to her nurse:
"The Queen should be made to sit down near this;
once she is seated, it must be held up toward the sky."
She did exactly as instructed;
at the very moment the weapon struck, the basket burst open.
Then, having been washed with a decoction water infused with healing substances,
healing substances were administered;
she was restored to health.
Jīvaka went into the presence of the king.
The king said,
"Jīvaka, have you completed the medical treatment of your stepmother?"
"Was it done by a god?
Did you see her naked?
"No, Your Majesty, I did not see her."
"How was it done?
He related exactly what had occurred,
and the king was filled with supreme wonder.
He said to the ministers,
"For a second time, perform the consecration of Jīvaka as the King of Physicians.
Then that man who had been afflicted with a tumor and told by Jīvaka that the medicines were difficult to obtain spoke up.
"Your Majesty, is this consecration being performed out of affection for your son,
or because of his medical expertise?
"Because of his medical expertise."
"If that is so, I have not been restored to health by him.
Jīvaka replied,
"O man, I did not perform your medical treatment."
"But I said, 'Those medicines are difficult for you to obtain. He asked,
'What kind of medicines are they for me?'"
Jīvaka said:
"If on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight a man who possesses only a single lump of food should die,
and while his body is being cremated in the cemetery, a brown mongoose and a sandalwood lizard fall upon the funeral pyre."
You devour those two;
the god Mahendra sends down rain,
yet you drink the water flowing from the cremation ground.
"Therefore, you eat kodrava rice and drink buttermilk; in this way, you will recover. Thinking this, I said that the medicines you require are difficult to obtain.
He replied, "Well said! You have understood it perfectly."
"This very thing was used by me.
Thereupon, having gained faith, he said:
"Your Majesty, this king of physicians is worthy of the consecration."
"Let him be consecrated!
Thus, for a second time, he was consecrated as the King of Physicians.
When Ajātaśatru, instigated by Devadatta as his evil friend, deprived his father—the righteous King of Dharma—of life, then a disease of the spleen manifested in him.
He gave the physicians an order,
saying, "Provide medical treatment.
They replied:
"Your Majesty, Jīvaka is the unsurpassed king of physicians and is the King's own brother.
While he is present, what power do we have to perform medical treatment?
Thus he gave this command to the ministers.
"Let Jīvaka be summoned, sirs.
He was summoned by them.
"Jīvaka, a disease of the abdominal tumors has appeared in me."
"Perform a medical treatment," [he said].
"I shall do so, Your Majesty," [the physician replied].
He then reflected:
A tumor is split by two causes:
either through excessive joy or through excessive anger;
thus, this is a being who commits evil deeds.
Thinking, "Whence comes this extreme joy of his?
He must be provoked in every way," he said,
"Your Majesty, I will provide a cure on one condition."
Upon hearing, "Eat the flesh of Prince Udāyibhadra," the king became enraged and said,
"Excellent!"
"I have deprived my father of life;
you too, Udāyibhadra, deprive [him] of life,
and I myself shall pass away by means of disease."
"You too shall become king," he said. He replied,
"Your Majesty, this is the remedy."
"It is not possible to remain at ease otherwise.
There is no love equal to that for oneself;
therefore, he accepted it.
Then Jīvaka, having adorned Prince Udāyibhadra with all his ornaments, presented him to the king, saying:
"Your Majesty, this is Prince Udāyibhadra; look upon him well, for you shall not see him again."
Then, having been shown [the way] by him, he was led to his house and settled there.
Thereupon, Jīvaka, seeking meat, went to the Śītavana cemetery;
and the Śītavana cemetery was not empty of a corpse.
Then, having taken the flesh of a corpse and prepared it with various special ingredients, he presented it to the king at mealtime.
Thereupon, as King Ajātaśatru took the bowl of meat and was about to eat, Jīvaka snatched it away and struck him on the cheek, saying:
"O evildoer, you have deprived your father, the righteous King of Dharma, of his life!"
"Now you are even eating the flesh of your own son!
Enraged, he said,
"If that is so, for what purpose was he killed?"
As his indignation arose, his internal tumor burst open; he was purged both upwards and downwards, and blood alone came out through his mouth. Upon seeing this, he fainted and fell to the ground.

Then, having bathed him once his life-breaths had returned through the sprinkling of water, he was given wholesome food, and he became as he was before. Thereupon, Jīvaka took Prince Udāyibhadra, adorned with all his ornaments, and approached the presence of the king.
Falling at his feet, he said:
"Your Majesty, this Prince Udāyibhadra cannot be made by me to deprive even an ant or an insect of life, much less the prince."
"However, I devised this plan thinking, 'He shall be treated by means of this method.
The king was filled with supreme wonder and gave an order to his ministers."
"Perform the consecration of Jīvaka as the King of Physicians.
Carried on the shoulders of the ministers with a great display of splendor, he was consecrated three times as the King of Physicians.
Thereupon, pride arose in Jīvaka.
"There is no physician equal to me; I am the foremost among those who treat the body,
and the Blessed One is the foremost among those who treat the mind."
At a later time, he approached the presence of the Blessed One;
however, due to his arrogance and pride, he did not perceive the truths.
The Blessed One reflected upon this.
"Jīvaka, the king of physicians, who has accumulated roots of merit, for what reason does he not see the truths? It is because of the intoxication of pride;
his pride must be removed."
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed Jīvaka, the king of physicians:
"Jīvaka, have you seen Himavat, the king of mountains?
"No, Venerable Sir."
"Take hold of the corner of the Tathāgata’s robe. He took it.
Then the Blessed One, taking Jīvaka, the king of physicians, went toward the Himalayas, the king of mountains.
There, various kinds of medicinal herbs were blazing like lamps.
The Blessed One said this to Jīvaka, the king of physicians:
"Take, Jīvaka, whatever medicinal herbs you desire."
“Blessed One, I am afraid.
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the yakṣa Vajrapāṇi:
“Go, Vajrapāṇi, and provide protection for Jīvaka.”
Having gone there, he gathered various kinds of medicinal herbs.
The Blessed One asked,
"Jīvaka, what is the name of this herb?"
He said,
"Blessed One,
such-and-such [a herb], by this method, is a pacifier of such-and-such a disease."
"This one also,
such-and-such, is the pacifier of such-and-such a disease," yet he does not know the names of the others.
The Blessed One spoke of that which Jīvaka did not know: "Jīvaka, this is such-and-such [medicine];
by such-and-such a method, it is the pacifier of such-and-such a disease."
"This too belongs to so-and-so," Jīvaka said;
"the Blessed One also knows medicine."

Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed Jīvaka, the king of physicians: "Jīvaka, a physician who extracts arrows, when endowed with four qualities, becomes worthy of a king, fit for a king, and is reckoned as one of the king's essential members."
By which four qualities is a physician who extracts arrows [a true healer]? He is skilled in the affliction and skilled in the origination of the affliction.
He is skilled in the abandonment of a disease that has arisen,
and skilled in its non-arising in the future once it has been abandoned.
How does he become skilled regarding disease?
In this case, a physician who removes arrows knows the affliction: "This is an affliction; it is of such a form and of such a nature. In this way, he becomes skilled regarding afflictions.
How does he become skilled regarding the origination of afflictions?
In this case, a physician who removes arrows knows the affliction: "This affliction has originated from wind, or it has originated from a disorder."

He is skilled in the origination of diseases, [knowing] whether they arise from phlegm, or from one's own conduct, or from the conduct of others, or from a combination of humors, or from the change of seasons.
How is he skilled in the abandonment of a disease once it has arisen?

In this case, a physician who removes arrows knows that "this affliction will be eliminated by means of an ointment, or a counter-ointment, or by emesis, or by purgation, or by upward purgation, or by downward purgation, or by nasal therapy, or by the application of incense, or by the treatment of sudation"; thus, he is skilled in the elimination of an arisen affliction.
How is one skilled in the non-arising of a disease that has been abandoned in the future?

Here, a physician who extracts arrows knows the disease and understands: "When such and such agreeable treatments are applied, this disease, once abandoned, will not arise again in the future. In this way, one is skilled in the non-arising of a disease that has been abandoned in the future.
It is so.
Thus, a physician who extracts arrows, endowed with four qualities, is worthy of a king, fit for a king, and is reckoned as a member of the royal entourage.
In the very same way, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, endowed with four qualities, is called the unsurpassed physician who extracts arrows.
And what are the four? Here, Jīvaka, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly awakened one, understands as it truly is: "This is the noble truth of suffering."

One understands, as it truly is: "This is the noble truth of the origin of suffering; this is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering; this is the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering. Indeed, Jīvaka, a physician who extracts arrows does not know the medicine for the abandonment of sufferings rooted in birth, nor does he know the medicine for the abandonment of sufferings rooted in aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair.
But the Tathāgata, Jīvaka, knows the medicine for the abandonment of sufferings rooted in birth;
he knows the medicine for the abandonment of sufferings rooted in aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair.
Therefore, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is called the unsurpassed physician, the remover of the arrow.
While this Dharma discourse was being spoken, the dust-free and stainless Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena arose in Jīvaka Kumārabhṛtya.
Then Jīvaka Kumārabhṛta, having seen the Dharma, attained the Dharma, known the Dharma, and plunged deeply into the Dharma—
having crossed over doubt, transcended uncertainty, becoming independent of others and no longer led by another— attained confidence in the teachings of the Master regarding all phenomena.

Rising from his seat, he draped his upper robe over one shoulder, bowed with palms joined toward the Blessed One, and said this to the Blessed One: "I have come for refuge, Venerable Sir; I have truly come for refuge. I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dharma, and to the Saṅgha of monks. May I be accepted as a lay follower."
"Support me from this day forward for as long as life lasts— me who have gone for refuge, am full of faith, and endowed with my very life.
Then Jīvaka, the king of physicians, bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and departed from the Blessed One's presence.
Because of its connection with snow, Himavat, the king of mountains, is perpetually cold; consequently, a condition of swelling has arisen in the Blessed One.
Jīvaka, the king of physicians, reflected:
"I myself shall attend upon the Blessed One, just as one would attend upon a universal monarch."
Then Jīvaka prepared thirty-two lotuses by treating them with substances that cause relaxation and presented them to the Blessed One,
saying, "May the Blessed One smell these. The Blessed One smelled them.
He obtained exactly thirty-two [instances of] rising;
then he asked the Blessed One,
"Has the Blessed One been properly purged?"
The Blessed One said:
"Jīvaka, there are those defects which have passed away but have not flowed out."
There are those who have flowed but not fallen;
there are those who have both flowed and fallen;
and there are those who have neither flowed nor fallen.
Jīvaka said,
"Blessed One, if that is so, then eat this jujube fruit with molasses and follow it with a sequence of rice gruel."

The Blessed One acted accordingly, and [the king] became healthy. It was the custom of Jīvaka that whenever he treated a king or a high official, the latter would grant him either a village or a choice village.
At another time, Jīvaka performed medical treatment for the King of Videha.
He gave him a cloak worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold].
Taking it, he approached the Blessed One.
Having approached and bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, Jīvaka Kumārabhṛta sat down to one side. Seated there, he said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable Sir, it is my custom that whichever king or royal official I treat provides me with a village or an excellent village."
I performed medical treatment for the King of Videha,
and he gave me a cloak worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold].
I now offer that to the Blessed One.
"Therefore, may the Blessed One accept it out of compassion.
The Blessed One accepted from Jīvaka Kumārabhṛta a large cloak worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold].
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was standing behind the Blessed One, holding a fan and fanning the Blessed One.
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda:
"Ānanda, take this cloak worth a hundred thousand [pieces of gold] and, for my sake, have it cut with a blade.
Then the venerable Ānanda, having taken it, went to a wide open space on the earth and began to measure it out.
He saw that many robes were being obtained.
Thereupon, he made a set of three robes for the Blessed One, an inner robe and an upper robe for himself, and a small bundle for the Venerable Rāhula.
Indeed, during that rainy season retreat, five hundred pieces of cloth were obtained for the Blessed One.
And there were many [offenses] for the community of monks.
The monks did not know how they should proceed.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Therefore, I authorize that monks, having cut householders' robes with a blade and discolored them, should wear them."
It was the custom of King Bimbisāra that, upon seeing a monk or a nun, he would dismount from the back of his elephant and perform a prostration at their feet.
On another occasion, having mounted his elephant, he set out to pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One. Then, while on the way, he saw an Ājīvika.
Filled with agitation, he descended from the elephant's shoulder and fell at his feet. Thereupon, those who were faithless reflected:
"The King is not only devoted to the monks."
"He has also placed his faith in the Ājīvakas.
But those who were faithful reflected:
"Surely the monk must be a god," and so, with great haste, they descended from the elephant's shoulder and fell at his feet.
With their minds filled with doubt, they said to the king,
"To whom did Your Majesty pay homage?
To a disciple of the Blessed One."
"Your Majesty, this is an Ājīvika; he is not a disciple of the Blessed One.
Then it occurred to King Bimbisāra:
"Let this very thing be my duty to perform."
He approached the place where the Blessed One was;
having approached and bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, Śreṇya Bimbisāra, the King of Magadha, said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, it is my custom that whenever I see a monk or a nun, I dismount from the elephant's back to pay homage at their feet.
Therefore, overcome with agitation, I dismounted from the elephant's back and fell at the feet of the Ājīvika.
'O Blessed One, would you out of compassion please establish some kind of mark upon the robes of the noble ones?'"
The Blessed One consented to King Bimbisāra by remaining silent.
Then King Bimbisāra, understanding the Blessed One’s consent through his silence, bowed his head at the Blessed One’s feet and departed.
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "O monks! (MSV II 50)

"Monks, that Ājīvika has been ruined because he accepted a salutation from one who had already seen the Truth. At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was standing behind the Blessed One, holding a fan and fanning the Blessed One.
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda.
"Ānanda, have you seen Mount Vaidehaka?
"No, Venerable Sir.
"Take hold of the corner of the Tathāgata’s robe."
He seized it;
then the Blessed One, by means of that very supernatural power, departed through the air above,
vanished from Rājagṛha, and alighted on Mount Vaidehaka.

Now at that time, having seen the fields of the people of Māgadha— level, with level surroundings, arranged in rows, and variegated by various patterns of design— the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, have you seen these fields, level, with level surroundings, arranged in rows, and variegated by various patterns of design?"
"They have been seen, O Venerable One.
Therefore, Ānanda, monks should cut and sew their robes in this manner.
The Elder Ānanda informed the monks.
