"You must tear these robes into pieces and sew them together in this manner. Having been instructed thus, the monks began to tear the robes and sew them;
they let the seams fall toward one side.
They did not look well. The Venerable Ānanda reflected:
"Even though it has not been permitted by the Blessed One..."
"It is possible that he will grant permission on this very account.
Therefore, he provided leaf-ends on both sides;
yet, as it still did not look beautiful without a border, a border was added.
Then, having made his decision, he presented it to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said: "Excellent, excellent, Ānanda! You have understood that which was not permitted by me."
Therefore, I authorize monks to wear robes after cutting them in this manner.
However, the monks began to cut and sew only one robe and then wash it,
leaving the remaining robes uncut.

Then the Blessed One, wandering on a tour through the Magadha country, arrived at Āṭavikā. He stayed at the forest of Agrāṭavika in Āṭavikā; because of its proximity to the river Āṭavikā, it was cool and breezy.
In the first watch of the night, the Blessed One put on his inner robe; in the middle watch, he put on his upper robe;
and in the last watch, he addressed the Venerable Ānanda.
"Ānanda, give me the saṃghāṭī.
Then the Venerable Ānanda, having washed his hands, placed the saṃghāṭī over the Blessed One.
That night was passed by the Blessed One wearing the three robes.
Then, when the night had turned to dawn, he reflected:
"Among those in the world who are delicate and seekers of pleasure,
I am the foremost."
"Knowing this—that 'I am able to subsist with even three robes, how much more so my disciples'—he addressed the monks:
'Therefore, monks, monks should wear the three robes when they have been cut [to size].
Thus it was said by the Blessed One: 'The three robes should be worn when they have been cut.'"
A certain monk did not possess a set of three robes; he had obtained a piece of cloth,
and he began to cut it.
The Blessed One arrived at that place and asked, "Monk, what is this? He replied,
"Venerable Sir, the Blessed One has stated that a monk must wear his three robes when they have been cut [to the proper size]."
"I have no third robe; while searching for one, this felt cloth has been obtained by me. I shall cut it and make a robe."
"O monk, this is not fit for cutting; rather, it is fit for sewing.
Having sewn it, wear it.
Having said this, he departed.
Having assembled the community of monks, the Blessed One sat upon the seat prepared before the community of monks.
Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the monks:
"Monks, because a certain monk has no robe, he cuts off his own hair."
Therefore, monks, there are five things that must not be cut off: all woolen cloth and all fine outer garments.
All woolen cloth,
all red-dyed cloth,
and all coarse blankets.
It should be worn after inserting pins.
The setting was in Śrāvastī.
King Prasenajit of Kosala had a chief minister named Mṛgāra.
He brought home a wife from a family of equal status.
He played, dallied, and enjoyed himself with her;
while he was thus playing, dallying, and enjoying himself, a son was born to him.
In this manner, up to seven sons were born;
for six of them, he established names according to their intended status.
As for the youngest, the name Viśākha was established for him. Later, when Mṛgāra’s wife passed away,
he provided wives for his six sons.
They remained preoccupied with their own adornments together with their respective wives;
they did not attend to household affairs.
The householder Mṛgāra, however, sat lost in thought with his cheek resting in his hand.
A friendly brahmin came to him; seeing him lost in thought, the brahmin said:
"Householder, why are you so preoccupied with anxiety?
These sons of mine are occupied solely with adorning themselves in the company of their respective wives;
they do not concern themselves with the affairs of the household."
"The house will fall into ruin.
He said,
"Why is Viśākha not given a marriage?"
Who knows? He might perhaps become even more wicked;
yet this too is not known: he might perhaps become even more excellent. If it is your consent, I shall search for a girl.
"Act accordingly.
Searching in due course, he arrived at Campā.
In Campā there was a householder named Balamitra.
He had a daughter named Viśākhā, who was endowed with beauty and youth, perfected in prudence and modesty, wise, and of quick wit.
Accompanied by several girls who were charming according to her own taste, she set out for a park.
And that brahmin arrived at that place.
He saw that girl and reflected:
"First, an examination of these very women must be made."
And he, intent on his concentration, was followed from behind by them as they moved with slow steps;
for women are generally of a fickle nature:
one among them ran, another leaped up, another stumbled, another laughed, another made gestures with her limbs, and another sang.
She performed these and other wicked deeds;
yet, being endowed with discipline and moving with a slow gait, she went along with them.
When they reached the park, those girls placed their clothes on the bank of a lotus pond and, suddenly plunging in, began to play.

As she entered the water, she lifted her garment higher and higher as she descended; likewise, with a perfectly tranquil deportment, she lowered her garment as she emerged. Then, having bathed and purified herself, she stood in one place.
Those maidens began to serve the attendants after they had first eaten themselves;
she, however, began to eat herself only after she had first served the attendants.
Then, having eaten and drunk and enjoyed the pleasure of the garden, they set out.
When it came time to cross a body of water on the way, those girls took off their sandals and crossed over;
she, however, continued on her way still wearing her sandals.
Then, they arrived at a grove.
Having taken up her parasol, she passed through a mango grove;
the other women cast away their parasols,
whereupon a wind and rainstorm broke forth.
Then the girl entered and remained inside a temple, while he was in the open air. Seeing such signs and movements of hers, the brahmin became curious and began to question the girl.
"Girl, whose daughter are you? "I am the daughter of Balamitra. "Daughter, I ask you this:"
"Therefore, you should feel some anger.
She, preceded by a smile, said:
"Father, ask."

"What is there to be angry about? Daughter, all these girls go along running, leaping, falling down, tossing their limbs, and performing various such ill-behaved actions; you, however, being endowed with discipline, proceed with a slow and measured gait. (MSV II 55)
"You are going to the park together with her.
She replied,
"All daughters are property to be sold by their parents."
"If, as I am flying up or falling down, my hand or foot should break, who would ask for me?
For I shall not be one to be supported by my parents for the rest of my life.
"Daughter, this matter has been well resolved."
I ask you this further question:
these girls, having set aside their garments in one place and being deprived of their second clothes, suddenly descended and began to play;
you, however, drew up your garment in accordance with the way the water entered.
"Father, women are endowed with a sense of shame and modesty;
it would be improper if someone were to see me uncovered.
"Daughter, who would see you there?"
"Father, at least let me be seen by you.
"Daughter, that is well; even that has passed.
Now I ask you this other thing."
"These girls first eat for themselves and only afterwards feed their attendants;
you, however, first feed your attendants and only afterwards eat for yourself.
Father, we live by the fruit of merit, and for us, every day is always a festival."
"These women, who subsist on the fruits of their low station, obtain a generous meal only once in a great while.
Daughter, even this excellence has passed away;
now I ask you this other thing."
"The whole world wears sandals on dry ground; you, however, wear them in water.
What is this?"
"Father, people are fools!
One should wear sandals even in the water.
For on dry land there are seen stumps, thorns, stones, pebbles, shells, gravel, and potsherds."
"But these are not seen in water;
therefore, sandals should be worn only in water, not on dry land.
Daughter, even this excellent [idea] has passed away."
I ask this further question:
these girls hold a parasol in the heat of the sun, while you, on the other hand, are in the grove under the shade of a tree;
what is the reasoning here?
"Father, people are foolish; the garden itself must be held as a parasol. For what reason? Because the garden is constantly filled with monkeys and birds."
The birds voided excrement and urine;
they dropped fragments of bone.
The monkeys also voided excrement and urine.
They cause fruits that are half-eaten to fall; because of their restless nature, they move from one branch to another here and there;
and they cause fragments of wood to fall.
And that [shade] does not exist in the open air;
it might occur only occasionally and would be light and easily blown away.
Therefore, one should hold the parasol only in a grove.
"Not in the open air.
Daughter, even this has been answered.
Now I ask you this other question."
"These girls have entered a temple during the wind and rain, while you remain in the open air.
Father, you should stay in the open air;
you must not enter a temple."
"Daughter, what is the logic here?
"Father, these empty temples are never truly empty; they are always filled with libertines, sons of Vāta, and rogues.
If someone touches my limbs when I have entered, it does not bring dishonor upon my mother and father."
"It is better to lose one's life in the open air than to enter an empty temple.

Then that brahmin, his mind filled with joy because his conduct had been approved, entered the residence of the householder Balamitra; and out of a longing to obtain the girl, he hurriedly offered a blessing.
He said, "May it be well.
The household attendants replied,
"Brāhmaṇa, it is not yet the time for alms."
"What do you seek? "I beg for a maiden.
"For what purpose?"
In Śrāvastī there was a chief minister named Mṛgāra;
his son was named Viśākha.
They said:
That family is indeed suitable for us;
what then is the problem? It is simply that the location is extremely remote.
He said:
"The girl must be given from afar.
For what reason?"
If she is happy, she will feel joy upon hearing it;
but if she is suffering, she will become weary from the act of giving, honoring, and showing respect, and there will be a depletion of wealth.
They said:
"If it is so, let her be given.
Then the brahmin, having said "May there be well-being," departed and in due course arrived at Śrāvastī.
Having dispelled the fatigue of the journey, he went into the presence of the chief minister Mṛgāra.
Then, having described the girl’s diet, her habits, her movements, the beauty of her form and youth, and her cleverness exactly as they were, he said:
"After wandering through various regions and districts with great exhaustion, I have obtained her with difficulty;
go now and marry her."

Then, having determined an auspicious day, lunar date, moment, and constellation, the chief minister Mṛgāra returned to Campā and married Viśākhā with great magnificence. Before her departure, she was instructed by her mother:
"Daughter, you must always pay homage to the sun and the moon."
The fire is to be tended;
the mirror is to be polished;
white garments are to be worn.
One should receive [alms], but not give;
one’s speech must be guarded;
and one should not rise to offer a seat to anyone.
"Sweet food is to be eaten;
one is to sleep comfortably;
a ladder is to be set up."
Then Mṛgāra heard of this;
he reflected:
"This girl is being taken away by one who holds wrong views."
Thinking, "I shall distinguish her from false views and cause her to adopt right view," he took her and set out.
Then her mother, her heart overwhelmed with affection and her eyes clouded with tears, embraced her neck and said, weeping aloud:
"Daughter, this is the last time you will see me."
Seeking to restore her consciousness, she said,
"Mother, I ask you:
were you born here, or rather in your own kinsmen's house?"
"Daughter, is that your house, or is this it? "This is it."
I too was born here;
I must dwell there.
Union is inevitably destined to end in separation.
"Be silent!
Why do you weep?
Then Mṛgāra set out by way of the dry land.

Viśākhā set out by boat together with her husband and the retinue she had obtained from her own home. There, a mare that had recently given birth was being boarded onto the ship; the foal, however, remained on the shore in distress.
"It will happen," she said;
yet, despite her efforts, she could not ascend, and a great clamor arose.
Viśākhā heard this.
She asked, "For what reason is there this clamor? They related to her exactly what had occurred.
Viśākhā said, "First mount the colt; he will mount it himself.
They did accordingly.
Having mounted it,
Mṛgāra then asked them:
"For what reason have you come so late?"
The mare would not board the ship. How, then, did she board?
Cāṇpeyikā explained a stratagem: "First, have the colt board."
The wise Cāṇpeyikā [arrived],
and eventually the caravan reached a place to stay for the night along the way; a bed was prepared for Mṛgāra on a mountain slope.
Having seen it, Viśākhā asked,
"Whose bed is this?
"Mṛgāra's."
"Remove it! For what reason?
If a landslide falls upon one who is asleep, he will certainly die, being pinned down."
"For as long as I live, this will be a source of ill repute for me:
that such a girl was married, yet before she had even reached her husband's home, her father-in-law passed away.
And so, that bed and seat were removed, and the roof-ridge collapsed.
A great crowd of people ran from all sides, crying out, "The householder has been seized!
The householder said,
"Sirs, do not be afraid."
"I am staying here.
They looked toward the bed;
the bed had been removed.
By whom?
By Viśākhā.
And the wise Cāṇpeyikā.
Once again, they arrived to stay in a dilapidated garden;
a bed was prepared for Mṛgāra in an empty temple,
and it was seen by Viśākhā.
He asks:
"Whose bed is this?
"The Noble One's."
"Remove it! For what reason?
If the temple collapses, then being pinned beneath it, he will die."
"Is it not as before that my fame has been restored?
Yet she has been removed,
and the temple has collapsed."
A great multitude of people ran forth as before, until they reached the wise lady Cāṇpeyikā.
Eventually, she arrived at Śrāvastī.
Once the fatigue from the journey had been dispelled and her friends, kinsmen, and relatives had been sent away, Viśākhā entered her own home in a manner befitting her family.
Karma is being performed.
Of Mṛgāra, six daughters-in-law take turns preparing food for the household members on their respective days.
Viśākhā was likewise appointed in that same manner.
"You must also take your turn on the seventh day," she said.
"Her turn will come.
She would take the remaining perfumes from her father-in-law, mother-in-law, and husband, form them into small cakes (*carpaṭikā*), and dry them every day.
From the barley meal she receives every day, Viśākhā sets aside a *prastha* and stores it;
she then mixes the remainder with ghee so that it becomes exactly that same amount.
As for the one who had come for wine, [she thought], "Tomorrow will be his turn."
Whatever was the master’s *nirmālya* (remains of offerings) and what she herself had placed there in the cool spot,
when the night had turned to dawn, she gave to the laborers myrobalan fruit, perfumes, flowers, food, and liquor.
They were deeply satisfied, thinking, "At long last we have been looked upon by the wife of the former householder."
On that day, they performed twice as much work as usual.
When Mṛgāra, inspecting the worksites at the appointed time, saw that a great deal of work had been accomplished,
he asked:
"Have you taken on other hired laborers? "No.
"What is the reason that today twice the amount of work has been done?
They replied:
"Noble lady, such is the food, such is the karma. What does this mean?
They then related to her in detail exactly what had occurred.
Mṛgāraputra’s wives were informed of this,
and they said,
"We too shall take [our husbands] away from their homes and do what is pleasing to our hired servants."
"May we also become dear to the Noble One and to you, his hired servants, just as Viśākhā has done.
Then Mṛgāra questioned Viśākhā.
"Daughter, how was the meal attended to by you?
She related it to him in detail,
and Mṛgāra was pleased.
Therefore, she alone was appointed to the management of the household affairs, and all the members of the family were addressed:
"Whoever among you is satisfied with what is given by Viśākhā should remain [in their position] or act in accordance with her until she has become the mistress of the house."
By her conduct, her way of life, and her gentleness, she satisfied everyone in the household.
At another time, swans came from the continent of Uttarakuru and, taking with them rice-grains of *śāli* paddy that grow without being ploughed or sown, set out;
meanwhile, a swan was staying in the king’s palace.
Upon seeing them, he let out a cry;
they too, unable to endure the agitation caused by the mutual trust born of their common origin, let out cries.
Rice stalks fell into the king’s foot-shrine.
Then the king gave one [daughter] to each of his ministers;
Mṛgāra gave his own share to Viśākhā.
She placed it in a casket and gave instructions to the farmers.
They, too, were exceedingly satisfied.
Having well-plowed a small portion of the field and knowing the proper time, they sowed it;
the god then sent rain at the right season.
The harvest was produced in accordance with the seed. In the following year, it was abundant; in the next year as well, it was even more abundant.
In this manner, until finally all the storehouses were filled with granaries brought by swans.
When King Prasenajit of Kosala fell ill,
he summoned physicians and questioned them;
they replied:
"Your Majesty, if rice brought by swans becomes available, you should prepare a broth with it;
by drinking it, you will recover.
The king summoned his ministers and questioned them.
"Sirs, I gave you the heads of rice brought by the swans;
what did you do with them?
To this, some replied:
"Your Majesty, we gave them to the temple," some said;
others said,
"We threw them into the fire."
Others said,
"We have fastened them to the gatehouse.
Mṛgāra said:
"Your Majesty, these were given by me to Viśākhā;
let me first ask what she has done with them.
He then questioned Viśākhā.
She said,
"Father, what need have we for rice brought by swans?
The king has fallen ill."
The physicians declared that the rice brought by the swans was [the best].
Thereupon, Viśākhā filled a golden vessel with the scum of the rice grains brought by the swans and sent it to the king;
the king consumed it.
He recovered his health. At another time, the people of the countryside sent two mares to the king:
a mother and her daughter.
In that situation, no one knew which was the mother and which was the daughter.
The king gave an order to his ministers:
"Gentlemen, having investigated thoroughly, report it to me."
The ministers, deliberating throughout the entire day, became exhausted; they had not reached a definitive conclusion. After a long time, Mṛgāra returned home.
Viśākhā fell at his feet and said,
"Father, why have you returned so late today?
He then related to her in detail everything exactly as it had happened.
Viśākhā said:
"Father, what is there to understand in this?
Equal and suitable food should be given by you both."
"The daughter will quickly devour her mother's portion;
the mother, being non-obstructive, will remain with her mouth open.
This is the sign."
Mṛgāra informed the ministers;
they, too, conducted the examination exactly as instructed.
Then, when the night had turned to dawn, they informed the king.
"Your Majesty, this is my mother; this is my daughter. The king asked, "How was this recognized by you?"
"Your Majesty, it was exactly so and so;
it was not fully understood yesterday.
Your Majesty, what power do we have to understand it?"
Viśākhā sent this message:
"The King says,
'Cāṇpeyikā is wise.'"
A certain man, having placed his blanket at a bathing place, bathed.
Then another man arrived;
wrapping his head with that blanket, he began to bathe right there.
Having bathed, that man rose and did not see the blanket.
The man said,
"O man, what are you searching for?"
"A woolen blanket! Where did you get this woolen blanket?
It seems that just as I descended after wrapping my head [in it], so too have you descended."
He said,
"This is indeed my blanket. A dispute arose between the two of them as to whether it was his or hers.
The two of them went into the presence of the king.
The king gave an order to his ministers:
"Sirs, having investigated the matter, restore [the child] to whomever he belongs."
They began to examine them;
one was questioned,
and he said, "It is mine."
Another was asked;
he replied, "It is mine.
"It is yours," [he said], "it is mine"—thus the day passed by.
The ministers, being weary after a long time, went home without having even deliberated upon the matter.
Viśākhā questioned Mṛgāra as before,
and he reported to her exactly what had occurred.
Viśākhā said:
"Father, what is there to be understood here? They should be told:"
"Let one take half and the other take half.
To whichever [monk] it belongs, he will say:
"For what purpose is my woolen blanket being cut?"
"He who has no sense of ownership will think, 'Let even half of this be mine;
what loss is there to me here?'—this is the test in this matter.
Having gone there, Mṛgāra reported this to the ministers.
"Your Majesty," [the minister replied] as before, up until the king said, "Cāṇpeyikā is wise. Then,
a merchant using the king's ship sent a sandalwood chest wrapped in cloth.
"It is not known which is its top and which is its root.
The king gave an order to his ministers:
"Investigate this!"
They deliberated for the entire day, but they did not understand;
after a long time, they returned home.
As before, Viśākhā questioned Mṛgāra up until [the point where] he related to her in detail exactly what had occurred;
Viśākhā then said:
"Father, what is there to be known here?
It should be thrown into the water;
that which is the root will be at the bottom."
"That which is the topmost becomes the uppermost;
this is the test in that regard," Mṛgāra informed the ministers.
As before, up until the king said,
"Cāṇpeyikā is wise.
In a certain small town, there was a householder.
He brought home a wife from a family of equal status;
however, he had neither son nor daughter. Longing for a son, he took a second wife.
Out of a jealous nature, that first wife administered a treatment intended to destroy her womb;
yet her womb became even more purified, and she became pregnant. When nine months had passed, she gave birth.
A son was born;
she reflected:
"This is a most wretched thing among enmities, namely, rivalry with a co-wife."
Surely another mother will have him killed by some means or other;
what will my master do, or what shall I do?
"And for how long must he be protected?
In every way, he must be given back to her. Having deliberated thus with her husband and having obtained his permission, she said to the first wife:
"Sister, this son of yours has been returned to you by me."
"Raise him up.
She reflected:
"The house belongs to her whose son he is."
"I shall raise him;
I will become the mistress of the house.
Thus he was raised by her.
His father had passed away,
and a dispute arose between the two of them concerning the house;
one of them said:
"The second one says, 'This is my son.
They went before the king,
and the king gave an order to his ministers."
"Go, sirs, and investigate. As they were investigating, the day passed away and they had not reached a conclusion;
after a long time, they returned home.
Viśākhā asks Mṛgāra, as before, up to: "What is to be understood in this matter?
They should be told: "We do not know whose son he is; whichever of you two is stronger, let her take him and go."
Seizing him by both arms, they will drag him away;
suffering in pain, he will weep,
and his mother will release him with gentle persuasion.
"Let me see him while he is still alive.
That other woman, being merciless, will not release him;
but when she is struck with the whips, then she will act according to the truth.
"This is the test in this matter," Mṛgāra informed the ministers;
[the account continues] as before, up until the king speaks.
"The wise one is Cāṇpeyikā.
Then, at another time, Mṛgāra fell ill;
his physician gave him medicine for one day, but he became ill again.
Viśākhā reflected:
"For what reason, father, do you become well on one day and then fall ill again on the second day? Those medicines by which you become well have been identified."
Then, having kept the physicians away, she herself performed the medical treatment;
he was restored to health. Mṛgāra reflected:
"What is the reason here by which I am healthy one day and ill the next;
and when the physician does not enter, I am always healthy?
He then questioned Viśākhā.
As before, up until the point where the wise Cāṇpeyikā [was mentioned]:
King Prasenajit of Kosala had an elephant trainer named Śrīvardhana.
On another occasion, he was dismissed by the king.
Viśākhā heard this,
and she said to Mṛgāra:
"Father, this will be the end and the destruction of all the ministers."
"You ought to ask the Lord Śrīvardhana for forgiveness.
He replied,
"Daughter, I forgive him."
Then the king was addressed by him:
"Your Majesty, Śrīvardhana is devoted to Your Majesty;
let this be forgiven."
The king said,
"Forgiven.
[The minister replied,] "Your Majesty, if it is forgiven, let those means of livelihood be given to him."
"So be it;
they have been given.
Śrīvardhana realized that Viśākhā had caused the king to grant him pardon.
He remained there with the intention of repaying her kindness.
At another time, Mṛgāra was afflicted by a human disease,
and Viśākhā attended to him.
He was ashamed.
She said,
"Father, why are you ashamed?"
"Why does my daughter not attend upon her father? Even so, she is ashamed. She reflected thus.
"He will not accept service from me;
I shall take him as a husband. Thinking this, she went to the house of Śrīvardhana.
Having greeted him with words of welcome, he offered him a seat;
Śrīvardhana’s daughter sat down,
and he said to her:
"Girl, take hold of Viśākhā’s feet.
Viśākhā said,
"It is possible that I myself must be the one to take hold of her feet," and having said this, she spoke further.
"May there be well-being for the son," Śrīvardhana said.
"What do you request?"
"A request for a maiden.
"For whose sake?
She replied:
"Of my father.
He remained silent.
Śrīvardhana’s wife said:
The Elder asked, "How is it given to him?
Viśākhā replied.
"For men are driven by wealth and youth; what is the use of deliberation? Let it be given!
Śrīvardhana said.
"Lady, Viśākhā has been very helpful to us;
let her be given [to us].
If it is so, let her be given."
Then she was married by Mṛgāra with great magnificence and splendor;
she began to attend upon him,
but Viśākhā did not do so.
Mṛgāra said,
"Daughter, give me an answer.
She replied:
She said,
"Father, let nothing be lost.
"Daughter, you who were [given] by your mother..."
"You have been instructed, yet you do not practice by undertaking even a small portion of it.
My dear, I practice by undertaking everything.
[The other replied: "As for what you say—that the sun and moon are to be honored—"
The mother-in-law and father-in-law are like the sun and moon to a young woman;
I pay homage to them.
As for what she says—that the fire must be tended—[it is so].
To a woman, her husband is like a sacred fire;
she should remain close to him and not stand too far away.
As such, I serve my master like fire. When he says, "The mirror must be polished," then this house, which stands in the place of that mirror, must be constantly smeared with cow-dung and swept clean.
Therefore, I indeed perform the maintenance of the house every day.
As for what he says— that white garments should be worn—
other clothes should be used for the household chores.
"Having put on white garments, service to the deity must be performed, and one should approach for one's own personal grooming.
This too I certainly do.
As for what he says—that it should be received and not given—I [do that as well].
What is to be accepted?
Harsh words from the world;
yet, not even a single harsh word should be spoken.
I also abide by undertaking this which he says: that speech must be guarded,
and secret words must not be made public.
In this regard, I certainly possess restraint over my speech;
for when he says that one should not rise from one's seat for anyone,
he speaks thus.
"You are a woman of good family; you must sit in a secluded place.
She replied, "I sit in a truly secluded place.
As for what he said, that "one should eat delicacies," [she answered:]...
"One should eat while hungry.
Thus, I always eat while hungry, even after my household members have already eaten.
As for what she says regarding "one should sleep comfortably":

"Having performed all the household duties and put away the utensils at night, you must prepare your bed in such a way that you do not rise again, thinking, 'This is well-placed; this is poorly-placed.
Therefore, I shall do exactly that."
As for what he says, "A ladder must be constructed," he speaks thus:
"You were endowed with the ten paths of action in former lives, by which you attained rebirth in the celestial realm and have now been born here in the world of humans."
Therefore, this is a land of action.
Here too, you must give gifts, perform meritorious deeds, and commit no evil.
For this too is a ladder made of merit, serving as a staircase to heaven.
"I shall accomplish this as well to the best of my ability.
Excellent, excellent, Viśākhā!
Your mother is wise."
"But you are more wise, for you have understood the mother's intentional speech.
Then it occurred to Mṛgāra:
"If the Blessed One would permit it, I shall proclaim Viśākhā as my mother. Having realized this, he approached the place where the Blessed One was.
Having approached and bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable Sir, is it permissible to declare one's daughter-in-law as one's mother?
The Blessed One said:
If he is endowed with five qualities— what are these five?
He attends to the sick.
He establishes them in suitable spouses,
provides for their livelihood,
and protects their wealth.
And he makes his arrangements with wisdom. The intermediate summary verse says: Attending to the sick, and [concern for] one's wife, life, and wealth.
One who inspires through wisdom—these five are remembered as mothers.
Then Mṛgāra approached King Prasenajit of Kosala;
having approached, he said this to King Prasenajit of Kosala:
"I wish [to do so]."
"Your Majesty, [I wish] to proclaim Viśākhā as my mother.
The king said, "Viśākhā also rendered service to me; I too shall ask my noble mother regarding that sister."
"I shall proclaim it.
Then she was questioned by the noble lady,
and she said:
"Announce it or not;
she is indeed your sister.
How so?"
Formerly, Brahmadatta entered into sexual union with a maidservant belonging to Arāḍa-Brahmadatta.
A son was born to her,
and he was given the name Balamitra. He was banished by the aged king on account of some legal matter.
Having gone to Caṇpā, he settled there;
his daughter is your sister.
Then the king, having placed her upon the back of an elephant, proclaimed:
"This is Viśākhā, the mother of Mṛgāra and the sister of King Prasenajit."
Having had a monastery built in the Eastern Garden, she dedicated it to the Saṅgha of monks from the four quarters;
likewise, it was recorded by the Elders in a Sūtra:
"The Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Eastern Garden, in the palace of Mṛgāramātṛ."
At another time, Viśākhā gave birth to thirty-two eggs.
When Mṛgāra heard this, he sat with his cheek resting on his hand, lost in thought:
"What kind of calamity has befallen the Beauty of the Land?"
Mṛgāra began to throw them away;
Viśākhā said,
"Father, do not throw them away."
"Announce this to the Blessed One.
He announced it to the Blessed One,
and the Blessed One said:
"Do not throw it away.
Having had that tortoise-shell box made with thirty-two compartments, he said, "Place one egg in each compartment for every member of the family."
And speak to Viśākhā:
"Touch her with your hand three times a day;
on the seventh day, they will burst open."
"There will be thirty-two princes.
He acted accordingly;
on the seventh day, they burst open.
Thirty-two princes were born;
they were raised, nurtured, and grew up until they became full-grown and possessed of heroic prowess.
On another occasion, having mounted their chariots, they went out and were returning.
And the son of the family priest, mounted on his chariot, was going out;
when they met, their chariot-poles and noses became entangled.
The son of the family priest said:
"Remove it!
they replied,
"You yourself must remove it."
"I am the son of the family priest," the man began to say;
thereupon, Viśākhā’s sons seized him by the tip of his nose and threw him down,
so that he fell into a heap of refuse.
With his head covered in ashes, he went into the presence of his father and,
his eyes clouded with tears, said:
"Father, the sons of Viśākhā have reduced me to such a state."
"Son, for what reason?
He related it in detail,
and he said:
"My son, if it is so that they are to be killed one by one,
do not grieve;
I shall devise a stratagem."
He remained intent on searching for their vulnerabilities.
At another time, a frontier town of King Prasenajit of Kosala rose in rebellion;
the king dispatched a military force against it.

They arrived having been struck down and slaughtered; in this manner, it continued until the seven positions of the army had been struck down and driven back. Then the king himself set out with his fourfold army.
The sons of Viśākhā also entered;
they saw him and said,
"Your Majesty is setting out to subdue the people of Kārvaṭika."
"Let it be, Your Majesty;
we shall depart.
Do as you have instructed."
He gave them a fourfold army, and having gone there, they subdued that mountain fortress;
taking captives, taxes, and tributes, they returned.
The domestic priest said:
"Your Majesty, these men are exceedingly valiant;
that which is difficult for Your Majesty to accomplish is easily accomplished by them.
This is what Your Majesty should consider."
For kings are always suspicious of crows;
keeping this in mind, he remained there and again questioned the domestic priest.
"How should one proceed in this matter?
He replied,
"Your Majesty, what is there to be done in this matter?"
"If it pleases them, they will depose the king from his kingdom and rule the kingdom themselves.
The king became even more distressed and reflected:
"It might indeed come to this."

He contemplated the arrangement of a means by which he might have him killed, thinking, "How should he be put to death? He did not ask anyone, lest there be a leakage of his secret counsel; as he deliberated on this himself, an idea arose in his mind.
"Having invited them right here, they must be killed. He sent word to Viśākhā: "The nephews must eat here."
She reflected:
"Tomorrow the boys will eat at their maternal uncle's place;
I too shall feed the community of monks headed by the Buddha. Having understood this, she approached the Blessed One.
Having approached and bowed her head at the feet of the Blessed One, she sat down to one side.
As Viśākhā, the mother of Mṛgāra, was seated to one side, the Blessed One gladdened her with a discourse on the Dharma as before, until he became silent.
Then Viśākhā, the mother of Mṛgāra, rose from her seat, and having extended her joined palms toward the Blessed One, [she addressed] the Blessed One.
He said this:
"May the Blessed One consent," as before, up until: "seated upon the very seat prepared in front of the community of monks."
And a messenger came from those kings, saying,
"Let the boys come.
Thereupon, they were rendered unconscious by the king using a mixture of *hālāhala* poison and other substances.
The heads were cut off;
then, having filled a chest and placed the head of the eldest son on top, they sealed it with a lac seal and sent it to Viśākhā.
Viśākhā reflected:
"Surely the King has sent clothing for his nephews;
I too shall clothe the community of monks headed by the Buddha.
Then, having perceived that the community of monks headed by the Buddha was seated comfortably, [he served them] with pure and excellent food, both solid and soft.
As before, having understood that the Blessed One had finished eating, that his hands were washed, and that the bowl was removed, she began to open the basket.
The Blessed One perceived this.
Knowing that if Viśākhā, who had not yet seen the Truths, were to witness the killing of her son, it was possible she would become unfit for the Truths, he said to her:
"Sit down first and listen to the Dharma; afterwards you may do as you wish."
Having prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One, she sat down before him to hear the Dharma.
Then the Blessed One, having understood her disposition, underlying tendencies, elements, and nature, brought about her vision of the truths as previously described.
Having seen the truths, she opened the basket and beheld the heads of her sons.
Then he said:
"Blessed One, all conditioned phenomena are thus impermanent.
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the monks:
"O monks, King Prasenajit of Kosala is the one by whom Viśākhā’s sons were slain. Had they not been slain,
with these very companions as his allies, he would have placed the entire earth within the palm of his hand."
Then King Prasenajit of Kosala, his body covered with dust, approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
To King Prasenajit of Kosala, as he was sitting to one side, the Blessed One said this:

“From where do you come now, Great King, with your limbs covered in dust? Venerable sir, those [attainments] belonging to anointed Kṣatriya kings who have reached the sovereignty, power, and valor of their realms, and who dwell having conquered a great circle of the earth—
The duties and affairs of state are manifold; having performed and completed them, I now return with my limbs covered in dust.
Therefore, Great King, I shall ask you this very question;
answer it as you see fit.
It is just as if, Your Majesty, a man were to come to you from the eastern direction— one who is trustworthy, reliable, steady, and not a deceiver of the world— and he were to say: "From there,
I am now coming to you from the eastern direction."
So I asked there: "From the great mountain— solid, without fissures, without cavities, well-rounded, and a single mass—
reaching from the earth up to the sky, and within this interval, all sentient beings, all living creatures, all beings, and everything..."
He comes along, crushing grass, wood, branches, leaves, and thatch.

"O Deva, whatever task you have to perform or whatever duty you must carry out, please do that. In this manner, a man should come from the southern, western, and northern directions, saying as before: "Whatever task you have to perform or whatever duty you must carry out, please do that."

"Thus it is, O Lord of the Earth, Great King: when such a great and terrible danger has arisen, when there is a cruel destruction of men and the attainment of human birth is so difficult to obtain, what should be done?

Venerable Sir, when such a great and terrible danger has arisen, when there is a cruel destruction of men and the attainment of human birth is so difficult to obtain, what should be done other than practicing for one's own welfare, practicing the Dharma, and practicing merit?"
"In order to apply oneself to wholesome conduct, to virtuous conduct, and to the teaching of the Buddhas—
why, O Great King, do you speak thus: 'In such a great and terrible danger as this,' and so forth, up to 'in order to apply myself to the teaching of the Buddhas'?"
Venerable sir, those various [conflicts] that occur among anointed Kṣatriya kings— who have attained power, strength, and valor through their territories,
and who dwell having conquered a great circle of the earth— consist of elephant-versus-elephant battles,
horse-versus-horse battles, chariot-versus-chariot battles, infantry-versus-infantry battles, and [battles] with secret spells.
There were battles of spells and battles of wealth;
at that time, those [opponents] were incapable, powerless, and lacking in prowess for battle.
Therefore, I speak thus.
"Venerable sir, when such a great and terrible danger has thus arisen— as previously described, up until 'to apply oneself to the teaching of the Buddhas'—
even so, Great King, living beings are constantly and perpetually being crushed by old age and death."

"Thus, O Great King, for a person who is being crushed by old age and death, there is nothing to be done other than the practice of purposeful conduct—as previously described—up until applying oneself to the teaching of the Buddhas. Having understood this, at that moment he spoke this verse:
"Just as great and vast mountains, having reached the sky..."
They advance from the great [host], grinding the earth;
there is no room there for elephants, nor for infantry, chariots, or horses, nor can victory be obtained there through battle of spells or by means of wealth.
In this way, old age and death crush all human beings:
kṣatriyas, brahmins, vaiśyas, śūdras, caṇḍālas, and pukkasas; those of immoral conduct as well as those endowed with virtue; likewise householders and those living at home.
Both the young and the old, as well as those of middle age.
For he crushes all and spares nothing;
therefore, a wise person, clearly perceiving his own welfare,
should place his faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the unsurpassed Saṅgha.
That practitioner of Dharma, whether by body, speech, or mind,
remains blameless in this world and rejoices in heaven after death.

Then King Prasenajit of Kosala, having rejoiced and delighted in the words of the Blessed One, bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, rose from his seat, and departed. The monks, overcome with doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts.
"Venerable sir, what karma did Viśākhā, the mother of Mṛgāra, perform,
as the ripening of which karma she gave birth to thirty-two sons, who became fierce and powerful?"
The Blessed One said, "By the power of a vow.
"Where was that vow made?
"In the past, monks, in the city of Vārāṇasī, a certain son of a householder passed away."
His wife was constantly longing for a son.

At that time, when the Blessed One Kāśyapa, the Perfectly Enlightened One, having completed all the work of a Buddha, had passed away into the realm of Nirvana without remainder— like a fire extinguished for lack of fuel—
there was a king named Kṛkin in Vārāṇasī.

By him, a stūpa made of the four jewels was erected for the Blessed One Kāśyapa, the perfectly enlightened one. There, that young woman who had been childless and longing for a son had grown old; she remained there, performing services for that stūpa.
Having made a request for alms from Chandaka, she performed an offering at that stūpa and made this aspiration:
"By this root of merit from the honors I have rendered to the Blessed One, Kāśyapa, the Perfectly Awakened One, may I have many sons. Having said this, she departed and entered the city.
There, a certain woman, being in labor and struck by painful sensations, cried out. Another woman asked her:
"For what reason is she crying?"
She reported exactly what had occurred.
She reflected:
"If I were to give birth, I too would experience such suffering."
Furthermore, when thirty-two companions again performed an offering at that stūpa,
that young woman was present right there;
having made the offering, she made a formal aspiration.
"By this root of merit, may we become great and possess supreme strength.
When they were asked by her, "Sons, what vow have you made? they replied:
They said, "Mother, this and that.
She said, "Sons, if it is so, then I myself would be your mother."
They said,
"Mother, let it be so," and having spoken thus, they departed.
She reflected:
"If even a single woman, giving birth once, cries out so piteously, overwhelmed by the sensation of pain, how shall I endure it when I must give birth thirty-two times?
And she reasoned in this way.
Near a stūpa, a hen laid her eggs;
within a mere moment, she had produced thirty-two chicks, yet she did not crow.
She reflected:
Thinking, "This is a skillful means for a beautiful birth," she fell down before that stūpa with intense devotion and began to make this aspiration:
"Just as this hen has given birth to thirty-two chicks in a mere moment, may I likewise give birth to thirty-two sons all at once."
"What do you think, monks?
That old woman who was the young girl at that time and on that occasion was none other than this Viśākhā. Those thirty-two companions were these very same thirty-two sons of Viśākhā."
Because she made that aspiration there, as the ripening of that karma, thirty-two sons were born.

"Venerable Sir, what karma was committed by Viśākhā’s sons, the ripening of which resulted in their being executed by King Prasenajit, who had neither harmed nor offended them? And [what of] their heads? (MSV II 79)
Having placed them in a basket, they were presented to Viśākhā.
The Blessed One said: "Monks, these very actions were performed and accumulated by these [beings], as previously stated, until: 'Indeed, for embodied beings, actions bear fruit.'"
Long ago, monks, in a certain mountain village there lived a liquor-seller. A large band of thieves, searching for intoxicants, approached him.
They asked, "Is there liquor? The brewer's wife replied, "There is," and she gave them the liquor.
There was no way out;
she pointed out a bull and said,
"Kill this one."
They said,
"There is no weapon;
she has taken it as a pledge."
The weapon was given;
they began to strike him down,
and as he was being killed, he cultivated conscious intent.
"Whatever I am to be killed, all of that shall be done by this wife of the vintner.
May I be reborn there, where, having cut off their heads and filled a basket with them, I might send them to her.
What do you think, monks?
He who was that bull was none other than King Prasenajit of Kosala at that time, on that occasion;
those who were the thieves were these very sons of Viśākhā;
and she who was the wife of the wine-seller was this very Viśākhā at that time, on that occasion—thus it is in detail.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, at the Squirrels’ Feeding Place. Now at that time, there was the hermitage of a seer possessing the five superknowledges. While he was wandering about, he voided urine on a patch of ground called Ciraṅkhala, not far from the hermitage.
By the turn of fate, a doe afflicted by thirst arrived at that place;
being tormented by thirst, she drank from it and smelled its female organ.
The ripening of the karma of sentient beings is inconceivable. She became pregnant,
and at a later time, having come to that very same place, she gave birth.
A boy was born;
having smelled him, she thought, "This is a being of a different kind," and having abandoned him, she departed.
Then, while that seer was wandering about the hermitage, he saw the boy.
He began to reflect, "Whose son is this?
and as he looked, he saw himself.
He then brought him into the hermitage, where he was suckled, nourished, and raised.
Because the head of that deer was such [a shape], it became known by the name Mṛgaśiras (Deer’s Head).
At a later time, that rishi passed away;
[the king] learned the spell for striking skulls with Mṛgaśiras.
Striking the skull, he interprets everything:
if the sound is sharp and piercing, it rises upward and he interprets it as rebirth among the gods;
if it is moderate, it rises upward and he interprets it as rebirth among human beings.
This is the sign of a happy rebirth; now, the sign of an unhappy rebirth:
if, for instance, his voice becomes faltering, he is one who goes downward, and it portends rebirth in hell.
Now, if the voice is of medium pitch, it indicates rebirth among those who go downward;
if it is of low pitch, it indicates rebirth as a hungry ghost (*preta*).
Then the Blessed One, knowing that the time for his conversion had come, addressed the Venerable Ānanda.
"Go, Ānanda, and prepare four seats for the stream-enterer, the once-returner, the non-returner, and the arhat.
"Very well, Venerable Sir," the venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One.
Having prepared the four seats, he went into the presence of that seer.
"Explain it!
He struck the skull of a stream-enterer and said, "This one has been reborn among the gods.
He did exactly the same for a once-returner.
It is exactly the same for a non-returner (*anāgāmin*).
When an arhat strikes his alms-bowl (*kapāla*),
he does not know or discern the object.
This thought occurred to him:
"Have I fallen away from that instruction, or was I not born into a noble family?
Or are the signs not such as they were, that I do not recognize his conduct?"
The Venerable Ānanda said:
"You have not exerted yourself in all branches of knowledge, which is why you do not understand his conduct.
First, study the entire science; afterwards, you shall explain it to the world."
Mṛgaśiras said,
"Have you seen anyone who has become accomplished in all the sciences?
He replied:
"There is a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly awakened one, who has reached the further shore of all knowledge. Then Mṛgaśiras approached the place where the Blessed One was.
Having approached, he said this to the Blessed One:
"O Lord, you know the destiny of a living being among animals, hungry ghosts, humans, gods, and in hell;
yet, when there is a failure in knowledge, I do not perceive the remaining conduct of sentient beings."
"O Lord, tell us of the vast and far-reaching shore of the great ocean of the three realms;
what is it that remains unknown, even after the victory over all rival teachers? Thus [he asked].
The Blessed One said:
Just as the course of a blazing fire struck by an iron hammer, which has gradually been extinguished, is no longer known; {cf. Uv 30.35}
Likewise, for those who are rightly liberated and have crossed over the flood of the mire of desire, there is no designated destination once they have attained the unshakable state. Thus it is said.
When this had been said, Mṛgaśiras spoke thus to the Blessed One:
"Venerable Sir, may I receive the going-forth and the full ordination into the state of a monk within the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya; may I lead the holy life under the Blessed One.
Thereupon, he was granted the going-forth and the full ordination by the Blessed One.
Having granted them the going-forth and the full ordination, and having stayed in Rājagṛha for as long as he pleased, he set out on a wandering tour toward Śrāvastī.
Traveling by stages on his tour, he arrived at Śrāvastī and dwelt there in the Eastern Park in the palace of Mṛgāra’s mother.
While walking in the open air, he saw that the constellations were displaced.
Having seen this, he addressed the Venerable Mṛgaśiras:
"Pay attention, Mṛgaśiras; after how long will the rain fall?"
He said,
"Venerable sir, this world is ruined, it is utterly destroyed!
It is as if the constellations have remained fixed for twelve years."
The Blessed One, having empowered the constellations to be equal, said,
"Know them again.
He replied:
After six years he spoke thus; when questioned again by the Blessed One, he said,
"In five years."
Thus it continued for up to seven days.
Then the Blessed One addressed the monks:
"Monks, protect the lodgings by covering them."
"Even today, the Lord will send rain in a torrent like a swarm of locusts;
those who bathe therein shall have no more eruptions, boils, or pustules."
"Thus indeed, the Mṛgaśiras constellations are fickle, unstable, and impermanent;
life too is fickle and unstable"— having been addressed in this way,
Mṛgaśiras became full of faith toward the Blessed One.
Having thus gained such serene confidence, he realized arhatship.
Then, experiencing the joy and bliss of liberation, he spoke this verse:
"The forest is the refuge of deer; the sky is the refuge of birds."
Dharma is the destination of those free from passion; Nirvana is the destination of Arhats. Thus it is said.

Viśākhā, the mother of Mṛgāra, heard that the Blessed One, while wandering on a tour through the Kosala districts, had arrived at Śrāvastī and was staying in our very own grove. Having heard this, she approached the Blessed One;
having approached, she bowed her head at the Blessed One’s feet and sat down to one side.
As Viśākhā, the mother of Mṛgāra, sat to one side, the Blessed One instructed, inspired, and gladdened her with a discourse on the Dharma as before, until finally he remained silent.
Then Viśākhā, the mother of Mṛgāra, rose from her seat, bowed with palms joined toward the Blessed One, and said this to him:
"May the Blessed One, together with the community of monks, accept my invitation for a meal at my home tomorrow."
The Blessed One consented, as before, up until the point where the water-jar was set down.
The maidservant sent by the Blessed One, who was to announce the time, announced the time.
When that maidservant went to the Eastern Grove, she saw the monks bathing naked through a crack in the door.
Having seen this, she reflected:
"Surely the noble ones have departed; this monastery has been seized by these Ājīvika Putramoṭikāputras.
She returned in great haste and said:
"Noble lady, you should know that the noble ones have departed;
this monastery has been seized by the Ājīvika followers of Putramoṭikāputra.
Viśākhā reflected:
"It is impossible, it is out of the question, that the Blessed One would depart without having accepted [the invitation] and eaten;
surely, monks, she must have seen him naked.
She then dispatched another man to announce the time.

"It is time, Venerable Sir; the meal is ready. Now, Blessed One, please do as you deem fit. [The text continues] as before, until, having understood that the Blessed One had finished eating, had washed his hands, and set aside his bowl, he sat down at the head of the assembly and said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, I wish to establish eight great gifts."

"Gifts for newcomers, gifts for those departing, gifts for the sick, gifts for those attending the sick, constant rice-gruel, constant medicine, the rainy-season robe (*varṣāśāṭī*) for the monks, and the bathing cloth (*udakaśāṭikā*) for the nuns.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
"Furthermore, Viśākhā, seeing what benefit do you give alms to a guest monk? Venerable sir, a guest monk is not skilled regarding the alms-round (*gocara*) nor skilled regarding the streets;
by partaking of my alms-food, he will become skilled regarding the alms-round."
"And you are skilled in the ways of the streets.
Well done, well done, Viśākhā! That matter is settled. For what purpose, then, do you give this gift for travel?"
"Venerable Sir, a monk who is traveling while seeking almsfood may become separated from his caravan;
being separated from the herd, he perishes.
May he, by partaking of my almsfood, not be separated from the caravan."
Nor is one who has strayed from the herd harmed.
"Excellent, excellent, Viśākhā! That matter is settled.
For what purpose do you perceive as beneficial that you give gifts to the sick?"
"Venerable Sir, a sick monk, while searching for almsfood, might become exhausted or even pass away.
If he were to partake of my almsfood, he would rise from his illness and dwell in comfort."
"Excellent, excellent, Viśākhā! That matter is settled.
Seeing what purpose do you give this gift as an attendant to the sick?"
"Venerable sir, a monk who attends to the sick, while seeking alms for his own sake, neglects the duties of the patient.
Having partaken of my alms-food, he will fulfill those duties.
Excellent, excellent, Viśākhā! This matter is also settled."
"Perceiving what purpose do you give this constant rice-gruel to the Saṅgha?
Venerable Sir, there are disciples of the Blessed One who have a keen digestive fire and those who have a weak digestive fire;
for those with a weak digestive fire, it serves to protect their digestion, while for those with a keen digestive fire, it serves to increase their strength."
Excellent, excellent, Viśākhā! That matter is also settled.
Seeing what purpose do you provide permanent medicine for the Saṃgha?
"Venerable Sir, there are disciples of the Blessed One who have many ailments and those who have few ailments.
Among them, for those with many ailments, [the benefit] has already been accomplished;
however, those with few ailments, by consuming it, will dwell in a state of greater physical ease."
"Excellent, excellent, Viśākhā! That matter is also settled.
With what purpose in mind do you give this rainy-season robe (*varṣāśāṭī-cīvara*) to the monks?
Venerable sir, this very day I have sent out a maidservant to announce the time."
Monks, she saw them naked while they were bathing; she came to me and said, "The noble ones have departed; the monastery has been occupied by the Ājīvika followers of Putramoṭika."
"Protected by my rain-cloak (*varṣāśāṭīcīvara*), they will bathe.
Excellent, excellent, Viśākhā! That matter is settled. But for what purpose do you intend to give bathing-garments (*udakaśāṭikā*) to the bhikṣuṇīs?"
"Venerable Sir, on this occasion there were many bhikṣuṇīs bathing naked in the Ajiravatī River.
Those laywomen, repeatedly scattering [water], pointed at the private parts of the bhikṣuṇīs with their fingertips.
Being thus pointed at, they became distressed."
"But they shall bathe while protected by my bathing-cloth.
Excellent, excellent, Viśākhā! Those eight bases of meritorious action which you have described are indeed seen here;
these are included within the seven material bases of meritorious action."

Regarding the seven material bases of meritorious action, it is not possible to grasp the measure of merit, saying, "The merit is this much," or "The fruit of merit is this much," or "The ripening of the fruit of merit is this much.
Rather, because of the abundance of merit, it comes to be designated as a "great merit" or a "mass of merit.
And this, Venerable Sir, I shall hear.
"Such-and-such a monk was predicted by the Blessed One as one who would attain [enlightenment] right here and now.

This monk also, through the abandonment of the three fetters, has become a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower realms, destined for full awakening, with seven births at most; having wandered among gods and humans seven times at most,"
Having passed through successive births and transmigrations, he will bring an end to suffering.
At some point he will come to Śrāvastī and will go there again;
he will enjoy my guest-meal, as before, up to and including the rainy-season robe.
And having heard that a certain monk, up to and including his water-strainer,
[had passed away], she again attained a sublime, wholesome, and noble joy and gladness associated with renunciation.
"Such-and-such a monk..."
The Blessed One declared:
"This monk, through the abandonment of the three fetters and the attenuation of lust, hatred, and delusion, will become a once-returner;
having returned to this world only once more, he will make an end of suffering."
"He too will perhaps come to Śrāvastī;
he will receive my guest-meal as before, up to the rainy-season robe (*varṣāśāṭī*) and the nun’s bathing-cloth.
Having heard this, I shall again attain a sublime, wholesome joy and gladness associated with renunciation.
"A certain monk has been declared by the Blessed One:
'This monk, through the abandonment of the five lower fetters, is a non-returner;
he will not come back again to this world.'"
"He too will come to Śrāvastī at some point and will go away again.
He will receive my provisions for guests, as before, up to the rain-cloak (*varṣāśāṭī*) for a monk and the bathing-garment (*udakaśāṭikā*) for a nun.
Having heard this, I shall once more attain a noble, wholesome joy and gladness associated with renunciation.
"A certain monk has been prophesied by the Blessed One:
'This monk, through the abandonment of all defilements, having realized arhatship, will enter the realm of nirvana without remainder.
He too will at some time come to Śrāvastī and will go away again."
"Having heard that my guest-food, as before, up to the *varṣāśāṭī* robe for a monk and the *udakaśāṭikā* for a nun [is provided],
I shall again attain a sublime, wholesome joy associated with renunciation.
Then the Blessed One, having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened Viśākhā, the mother of Mṛgāra, with a discourse on the Dharma, rose from his seat and departed.
Then the Blessed One, having stayed at Śrāvastī for as long as he pleased,
set out on a wandering tour toward Vaiśālī.
Traveling by stages on his tour, he eventually arrived at Vaiśālī.
The Blessed One was staying at Vaiśālī, in the Gabled Hall on the bank of the Markaṭahrada lake.
Then, having dressed in the forenoon and taken his bowl and robe, the Blessed One entered Vaiśālī for alms.
At that time, a great many monks were at the gate of the monastery cleaning, drying in the sun, and sprinkling with water the lodgings defiled by impurities.
The Blessed One saw many monks at the gate of the monastery cleaning, warming in the sun, and repairing beds and seats that were stained with impurities.
Having seen this, it occurred to him:
"Even though faithful brahmins and householders give gifts by repeatedly squeezing out their own skin, flesh, and blood."
Knowing that they were performing meritorious deeds and yet consuming them with moderation and discernment, the Blessed One,
having walked for alms in Vaiśālī and finished his meal, returned from his alms-round after the meal; he put away his bowl and robe, washed his feet, and entered the monastery for seclusion.
Then, in the evening, the Blessed One rose from his seclusion and sat down on the seat prepared for him in front of the community of monks.
Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the monks:
"In this regard, monks, having dressed in the forenoon and taken my bowl and robe, I entered Vaiśālī for alms."
"Monks, I saw many monks at the gate of the monastery cleaning, drying, and repairing beds and seats stained with impurities.
Upon seeing this, it occurred to me:

'Even when faithful brahmins and householders give gifts and perform meritorious deeds by repeatedly pressing out their own skin, flesh, and blood, the monks must do so with moderation and careful reflection.'"
They partook [of the food].

"Excellent, monks, is the moderate consumption of what is given in faith, the timely consumption, the consumption with intervals, the consumption in measured amounts, and the consumption in moderation.
Then the Blessed One, having spoken in praise of the moderate consumption of what is given in faith and so forth, addressed the monks:

"Therefore, monks, one must not use the bedding and seats belonging to the Saṅgha without a spread, nor bedding and seats stained by impurities; they must be cleaned at that very moment, otherwise there is an offense of transgression. Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the forenoon and taken his bowl and robe, entered Vaiśālī for alms with the venerable Ānanda as his attendant monk.
The Blessed One saw a certain man with a black back.
