"Who would do such a thing?"
"However, you have invited an elderly brahmin; I have not invited him. Having said this, he took that cloth and departed even before the other.
That brahmin began to revile him.
What do you think, monks?
That brahmin who was old at that time and on that occasion was none other than this Upananda.
Even then, though uninvited, he joined in the gains of another; so it is even now.
The setting was Śrāvastī. In a certain small town there was a householder.
He had a monastery built.
There, a certain monk entered the rains retreat;
he was endowed with great diligence.

Therefore, that monastery was plastered and swept every day. Furthermore, that monastery was established on a beautiful, secluded, and open plot of ground, adorned with various trees, resounding with the cries of swans, cranes, peacocks, parrots, mynas, and cuckoos,
and graced with diverse flowers and fruits.
Meanwhile, a caravan leader of vast wealth arrived at that monastery for the night.
Having seen the splendor of the monastery and the beauty of its groves, he was filled with faith; without even seeing the community of monks, he sent a great amount of offerings intended for them.
He then rose in the middle of the night and departed.
That monk, being full of remorse, did not accept the property of the Saṃgha out of regret, thinking, "This is the Saṃgha's gain," and instead sought only other monks to distribute it.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One said:

If a monk has entered the rains retreat having taken refuge even in a cow-dung hut, and if Brahmins or householders there offer a gift intended for the Saṅgha— whether small or great— it belongs only to those who reside there, whether they be one, two, or many.
No remorse should be felt in this matter.
Summary verse:
[The portion] to be given to those who have split [the community], the share of the Ṛṣila, and the wandering.
One should have the robe of the Saṅgha made from eight portions of the gain.
The setting was Śrāvastī. The Venerable Upāli questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, might the Saṃgha be split during the rainy season?"
"Should the gain be given or should it not be given?
The Blessed One said, "Upāli, it should be given to some; it should not be given to others."
To whom should it be given?
To one who belongs to the side of the Dharma. // 1 //
"Venerable Sir, during the rains retreat, a monk renounces the training and reverts to a lower state.
Should the gains be given to him or not?
Upāli, they should be given to some and not given to others."
To whom should it be given?
To that very person again. // 2 //
"Venerable Sir, if a monk should pass away during the rainy season,
should his gains be given out or not?
Upāli, they should be given to some and not given to others."
To whom should it be given?
To him who has the greater share. // 3 //
In a certain mountain hamlet there was a householder who had built a monastery fully equipped with all necessary articles.
And the Venerable Śāriputra, while wandering on a tour through the countryside, arrived at that monastery.
After that householder had fed him, he covered him with five hundred pieces of cloth;
having given those five hundred pieces of cloth to that very monastery, he departed.
Eventually, his two co-residents, Ṛṣila and Ṛṣidatta, while wandering on a journey through the countryside, arrived at that same village.
Those two were also fed by that householder and presented with five hundred garments;
they were then addressed by the monks:
"Venerable ones, five hundred pieces of cloth were obtained by your preceptor from that householder;
they were divided by us alone.
Now, this gain likewise belongs to us alone."
The two of them said:
"The preceptor is renowned and possesses great merit;
perhaps he has at some time expressed his approval of you."
They began to wake up.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
Monks, there are these eight kinds of acquisitions.
What are the eight?
An acquisition brought within the boundary.
That which is brought about by action;
that which is brought about by reliance;
that which is designated by the Saṃgha.
The one prescribed for monks;
the one pertaining to the rainy season;
the one in person.
And there is the rejection [of the boundary].
What is the gain brought by the boundary?
It is, for example, when there is a single residence with a single *poṣadha*.
Whatever gain accrues to those two monasteries belongs to the monks residing in both monasteries.
For sometimes the monks residing there enter the rainy season retreat under a single *poṣadha*.
Whatever gain is obtained there, which is given to this very monastery, must indeed be consumed by the monks residing in that [specific] monastery alone.
Because they share a single *poṣadha*, this is called "gain acquired through the boundary.
What is "gain acquired through ritual action"?
It is when monks, having made such a formal agreement (*kriyākāra*), enter the rains retreat.
"Such-and-such a family is yours;
such-and-such a family is ours.
"The middle [of the town] consists of the streets, lanes, crossroads, and junctions."
If those brahmins and householders,
having fed both the monks who have accepted the invitation and those who have not at the residence of those who have accepted the invitation, bestow the gains upon the invited monks alone,
[but provide] water for the invited monks alone.
To whom does the gain accrue? Only to those who have formally undertaken [the precepts]. // 1 //

When residents of a monastery who have entered a formal agreement feed both monks who have entered such an agreement and those who have not, and then bestow the gains upon those who have entered the agreement while giving water to those who have not,
to whom does the gain accrue?
Only for those who have formally undertaken [the vows]. // 2 //

When the residents of a monastery have fed both the *upagataka* (initiated) and the *anupagataka* (non-initiated) monks, they then provide drink to the *upagatakas* and give alms to the *anupagatakas*. To whom does the alms belong? To whom does it accrue?
Only for those who have formally undertaken [the precepts]. // 3 //

When residents of a monastery who have formally entered the rainy season retreat feed both monks who have entered the retreat and those who have not, and they give the offerings to those who have not entered,
as well as the drinking water to those who have not entered—
whose acquisition of the merit does this accrue?
Only for those who have formally undertaken [the precepts]. // 4 //
When residents of a monastery who have formally accepted an invitation feed both monks who have accepted the invitation and those who have not, and then present the gain at the head of the assembly,
as well as water for the residents who have accepted the invitation—
whose acquisition of the gain does it belong to?
Only for those who have formally undertaken [the precepts]. // 5 //
When those who have formally entered the residence (the *upagatakas*) feed both the monks who have entered the residence and those who have not, and then bestow the gains upon the *upagatakas*,
including water for the elders at the end of the meal—
whose acquisition of the gains does it accrue to?
Only for those who have formally undertaken [the vows]. // 6 //
The residents of the monastery, having fed both the formally enrolled monks and those who were not formally enrolled, offer the gain at the head of the assembly to the formally enrolled monks,
while water is offered to those who are not formally enrolled.
To whom does the gain belong?
One enters [the vows] only for those who have already formally accepted them. // 7 //

When those residing in a monastery where [the formal agreement] has been accepted feed both the monks who have accepted the agreement and those who have not, and then present the gains to the monks who have not accepted the agreement—
[including] water at the end of the meal for the elders—
to whom does the gain accrue?
Only for those who have formally undertaken [the precepts]. // 8 //

When residents of a monastery who have entered into a formal agreement feed both the monks who are under such an agreement and those who are not, and they distribute the gains as well as drinking water to both the monks under agreement and those who are not,
to whom does the gain accrue?
Only for those who have formally undertaken [the vows]. // 9 //

Just as there are nine permutations regarding those residing in a monastery who, having fed both the invited and the uninvited monks, [give the gains to the invited], so too there are nine permutations regarding those residing in a monastery who, having fed the uninvited monks, [give the gains to the invited].

If those brahmins and householders, having fed both the invited and the uninvited monks in the streets, lanes, crossroads, and junctions, bestow the gains upon the invited; [then they incur an offense].
The water belongs only to those who have formally accepted [the invitation].
To whom does the gain accrue? It accrues to both. // 1 //

In the streets, lanes, crossroads, and junctions, having fed both the *upagata* (ordained) and the *anupagata* (unordained) monks, they provide the gains (*lābha*) to the *upagata* monks and water to the *anupagata* monks.
To whom does the gain belong?
It belongs to both as well. // 2 //

In the streets, lanes, crossroads, and junctions, having fed both the *upagata* (those who have joined the community) and the *anupagata* (those who have not joined) monks, they give the gains to the *anupagata* monks and water to the *upagata* monks.
To whom does the gain accrue?
Of both as well. // 3 //
Having fed the monks who have arrived at the main roads, streets, crossroads, and junctions, they then provide gains for those who have not arrived,
as well as water for those who have not arrived.
To whom does such a gain accrue?
Of both as well. // 4 //
In the streets, lanes, crossroads, and junctions, having fed both resident and non-resident monks, they offer the gains at the head of the assembly;
[they also provide] drinking water for the residents.
To whom does the gain accrue?
Of both as well. // 5 //
Having fed both ordained and non-ordained monks at the roads, streets, squares, and crossroads, they then bestow the gains upon the ordained ones.
When water is offered at the end of the meal,
to whom does the gain accrue?
Of both as well. // 6 //
In the streets, lanes, crossroads, and junctions, having fed both those who have entered the order and those who have not, they offer the gains at the end of the assembly;
[but] for those who have not entered, there is only water.
To whom does the gain accrue?
Of both as well. // 7 //

Having fed both those who have entered the order and those who have not at the carriage-roads, streets, crossroads, and junctions, they then bestow the gains upon those who have not entered the order;
[and] water at the end of the assembly for the elders.
To whom does the gain accrue?
Of both as well. // 8 //

Having fed both the initiated and the uninitiated monks at the carriage-roads, streets, crossroads, and junctions, they present the gains and water to the initiated and the uninitiated at the end of the assembly of elders. To whom does the gain belong?
Of both as well. // 9 //
This is called gain derived from activity.
What is gain derived from reliance?
When a monk enters the rains retreat in dependence upon a woman, a man, or a paṇḍaka, whatever gain they give belongs to that very person alone.
This is called gain obtained through dependence.
What is gain designated for the Saṃgha?
It is that gain which is fixed and not distributed.
This is called property designated for the Saṃgha.
What is property designated for individual monks?
It is that property which is fixed and not distributed.
Whether it be in a dwelling, a monastery, or a gabled chamber that has been assigned,
it belongs to whichever monk resides there;
this is called "gain assigned to a monk."
What is the rainy-season gain?
It is the gain designated by donors for the community of monks who have resided during the rains;
this is called the rainy-season gain.
What is gain obtained in the presence?
That gain which is undetermined and unelaborated;
this is called gain obtained in the presence.
What is the attainment of the prophecy?
It is the attainment bestowed upon birth, enlightenment, the turning of the wheel of Dharma, and parinirvāṇa.
If it cannot be given at the four great caityas, it may be given at one single great caitya, and not elsewhere.
This is called the attainment of a refusal.
The summary verse:
They die; those who have been suspended; and the vessel for mixed [cases].
Those who have been suspended as novice monks drive others away and even cause them to die.
The setting was Śrāvastī.
The Venerable Upāli questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, it may happen that in one residence many who have been suspended (utkṣiptaka) and many who are in their natural state (prakṛtisthaka) dwell together."
If one who has been suspended dies, to whom does the gain consisting of his personal effects belonging to the deceased accrue?
To those who are in their natural state, Upāli. 1.

"Venerable Sir, there are two who have been suspended and many who are in their natural state. If one who has been suspended dies, to whom does the gain consisting of his deceased personal effects accrue?"
Only for those who are in their natural state. // 2 //
There are many who have been suspended (utkṣiptaka) and few who remain in their natural state (prakṛtisthaka).
A suspended monk passes away;
to whom does the gain consisting of his deceased personal effects belong?
Only for those who are in their natural state. // 3 //
"Venerable sir, it may happen that in a certain residence many who have been suspended (utkṣiptaka) and many who are in their natural state (prakṛtisthaka) dwell together.
If one of those in their natural state passes away,
to whom does the acquisition consisting of the deceased's requisites belong?"
Of those who are abiding in their natural state. // 1 //

There were many who had been suspended (utkṣiptaka) and two who were in their natural state (prakṛtisthaka). One who was in his natural state passed away. To whom does the acquisition of the deceased's requisites (mṛtapariṣkāra-lābha) belong?
Of that one [element] which is in its natural state. // 2 //
There are many who have been suspended (utkṣiptaka) and one who remains in his natural state (prakṛtisthaka).
If that person remaining in his natural state dies,
to whom does the gain (lābha) accrue?
Among those who have been suspended, he is the one who first renounces his evil view. // 3 //
If a novice who is not yet a full member comes to the residence of those who are full members and passes away,
the full members must send a messenger to those who are not full members,
saying: "A novice among you has died."
"Take away his bowl and robe! Thus they, being those who had accepted [the invitation], divided them; it was not properly divided, it was wrongly divided.
Those who have not yet accepted [the formal act] divide [the goods]; what has been divided is properly divided. Those who have mixed [the goods] divide them.
What was not distributed is poorly distributed;
they dedicate it to the Saṅgha of monks from the four quarters, and thus it is well dedicated. // 1 //
(MSV II 115) If a novice who is not yet enrolled (*anupagataka*) comes to the residence of those who are enrolled (*upagatakānām*) and says, "Venerable sirs, please restore me;
I shall become enrolled," and he should die before being restored, [what is the case?]
Those who have accepted [the invitation] should send a messenger to those who have not accepted it, saying:
"A novice among you has passed away;
please take his bowl and robes."
Those who have formally entered the community divide [the goods];
this is not a distribution, it is an improper distribution.
Those who have not formally entered the community divide [the goods].
What has been distributed is well-distributed;
what the *miśraka*s distribute is not distributed, and is therefore poorly distributed.
They dedicate it to the Saṅgha of monks from the four quarters; it is well-dedicated. // 2 //
If a monk who is not a member of the community should come and die in the residence of those who are members of the community,
the members of the community must send a messenger to those who are not members, saying:
"A fellow practitioner of yours has passed away."
"Take away his bowl and robe! Thus they, having agreed, divided [the property]; it was not properly divided, it was wrongly divided.
Those who have not yet accepted [the formal act] divide [the property]; it is well-divided when divided by those who have accepted it;
those who mix [the property] divide it.
It was not properly distributed; it was wrongly distributed. They dedicate it to the Saṃgha of monks from the four quarters.
It is well-dedicated. // 3 //
If a monk who has not yet been reconciled comes to the residence of those who have been reconciled and says, "Venerable sirs, please restore me;
I shall become one who is reconciled," and he should die before being restored; [he is considered to have died while still unreconciled].
Those who have already accepted [the invitation] should send a messenger to those who have not yet accepted, saying:
"A fellow practitioner of yours has passed away;
please take his bowl and robes."
Those who have formally accepted [the invitation] divide [the goods]; this is undivided and improperly divided. Those who have not formally accepted [the invitation] divide [the goods].
What has been distributed is well-distributed;
what the *miśrakas* distribute is not distributed, and is therefore poorly distributed.
They dedicate it to the Saṅgha of monks from the four quarters; it is well-dedicated. // 4 //
If a novice who has been admitted [into the community] should die while staying in the residence of those who have not yet been admitted,
the non-admitted ones must send a messenger to those who have been admitted, saying:
"The novice among you has passed away."
"Take away his bowl and robe. Those who were not yet ordained divided them; it was an improper division, an ill-apportioned distribution.
Those who have formally accepted [the rules] divide [the goods]; what has been divided is properly divided. Those who mix [the goods] divide them.
What was not distributed is poorly distributed; when they dedicate it to the Saṅgha of monks from the four directions, it is well dedicated. // 1 //

If a novice who is a *upagataka* (one who has entered the community) comes to the residence of those who are *anupagatakas* (those who have not yet entered) and says, "Venerable sirs, please restore me;
I shall become an *anupagataka*," and he should die before being restored, [what is the case?]
Those who have not yet joined [the community] should send a messenger to those who have joined, saying:
"A novice among you has passed away;
take his bowl and robes."
Those who have not formally joined the community divide [the property]; that which is undivided is improperly divided. Those who have formally joined the community divide it.
It is properly distributed if it is well-distributed;
they distribute it improperly if they mix [the portions]; it is wrongly distributed if it is not distributed at all.
They dedicate it to the Saṅgha of monks from the four quarters; it is well-dedicated. // 2 //
If a monk who has been formally accepted (an upagataka) should die while staying in the residence of those who have not yet been formally accepted,
the latter must send a messenger to those who have been accepted, saying:
"A fellow practitioner of yours has passed away."
"Take away his bowl and robe. Those who were not yet ordained divided them; this was an improper division. It was wrongly divided.
Those who have formally accepted [the rules] divide [the goods]; it is well-divided when divided by them. Those who mix [the goods] divide them.
What was not distributed is poorly distributed;
they dedicate it to the Saṅgha of monks from the four directions; this is well-dedicated. // 3 //
If a monk who has been suspended (upagataka) comes to the residence of those who have not yet suspended him (anupagataka) and says, "Venerable sirs, please reinstate me;
I shall become one who is no longer suspended," and he should die before being reinstated; [he is considered to have died while still suspended].
Those who have not yet joined [the community] should send a messenger to those who have joined, saying:
"A fellow practitioner of yours has passed away;
take his bowl and robes."
Those who have not formally entered the community divide [the property]; that which is undivided is improperly divided. Those who have formally entered the community divide it.
It is properly distributed if it is well-distributed;
they distribute it improperly if they distribute it by mixing [the portions]; it is wrongly distributed if it is not distributed at all.
They dedicate it to the Saṅgha of monks from the four directions; it is well-dedicated. // 4 //
The summary verse:
Upananda’s residence must be destroyed; he is a distraction to the community.
After my passing, there shall be no giving away of these three types of men.
The setting was Śrāvastī.
A boil arose on the head of Upananda;
he went to the presence of a physician.
"O gentle-faced one, prescribe a medicine for me.
He replied, "Noble sir, drink ghee;
you will recover."
Upananda reflected:
"If I drink it this very day, I shall recover this very day;
but on what pretext shall I have ghee or clothes prepared tomorrow?"
"I shall meditate for as long as I desire, and afterwards I will drink.
His great merit was recognized;
therefore, he dispatched his co-residents and disciples in all directions.
They had many jars of ghee and cloths for bandaging wounds prepared by them.
On the second day, the physician arrived and asked, "Noble sir, are you recovered?"
"You have drunk ghee.
"Worthy sir, I have not drunk it.
"Noble one, you have done what is not good."
"Drink double today," he said.
His co-residents and disciples were told this, and they replied, "We have heard what the physician has said, Preceptor; we have heard it."
"This disease of mine has increased;
provide me with plenty of ghee and cloths for bandaging my wounds.
They provided him with even more ghee and cloths.
Out of excessive greed, thinking, "It will be tomorrow," he did not drink even on that day;
consequently, his illness became severe.
When the physician arrived once again and questioned him:
"Noble sir, the ghee was drunk.
"Good sir, it was not drunk.
"Noble sir, you have done what is not right."
He said,
"Noble sir, today I shall drink three times as much.
The physician said:
"Noble one, even if you remain submerged inside a chest of ghee, you still have no life.
He replied,
"O Yamadaṇḍika, as you are!"
"Placing my foot upon your neck, I shall drink the ghee and live! Having said this,
the physician uttered a "hum" and departed in indignation.
Then Upananda, having filled a vessel with ghee, drank it;
he suffered from dysentery and passed away.
He possessed abundant gold, three hundred thousand pieces of gold.
The first [offense] is regarding the bowl and robe; the second is regarding medicine for the sick;
the third is regarding what has been prepared or not prepared.
The ministers heard this and informed the king:
"Your Majesty, the noble Upananda has passed away."
He possesses abundant gold— three hundred thousand pieces of gold. Therefore,
you should grant him your permission.
The king said,
"If that is so, go and seal his cell."
The monks took him and went to the cremation ground;
having returned, they sealed the cell.
After the monks had performed the funeral rites for him at the cremation ground, they returned to the monastery.
They saw a shelter sealed with the king’s seal.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda.
"Go, Ānanda, and in my name ask King Prasenajit after his health,
and speak thus:"
"Great King, at whatever time you have royal business to attend to,
do you look upon the monk Upananda at that time? Or at whatever time you have a wedding or a marriage ceremony to oversee, do you look upon Upananda at that time?"
Or perhaps he has been invited by you for as long as life lasts to provide the requisites of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal provisions for the sick;
or perhaps he has provided nursing care for one who was ill.
If he should say, "No," [then it is not an offense].
He should be told:
"Great King, the household affairs of laypeople are one thing; those of the renunciants are another."
"Remain with little concern;
this gain accrues to your fellow practitioners.
Be free from involvement."
"So be it, Venerable Sir," the venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One, and having departed from him, he approached King Prasenajit of Kosala.
Having approached, he reported everything exactly as he had been instructed.
The king said:
"Venerable Ānanda, let it be as the Blessed One commands;
I shall cease my activity.
Then the Venerable Ānanda reported the king's reply to the Blessed One.

Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, divide the personal effects of the deceased monk Upananda. The monks brought them into the midst of the Saṃgha, sold them, and divided the proceeds.
The monks of Sāketa heard that Upananda had passed away and that his abundant gold— three hundred thousand pieces of gold— had been divided among the monks.
Hurrying, they arrived at Śrāvastī and said,
"Venerable Upānanda is also our fellow-practitioner;
may we also receive a share of the gains belonging to him."
The monks, having caused [the property] to be brought down, divided it once again together with them.
In this manner, the monks residing in six great cities assembled:
those from Vaiśālī, those from Vārāṇasī, those from Rājagṛha, and those from Cāmpā.
The monks repeatedly cast lots and distributed [the goods].
While casting lots and distributing them, the monks neglected their formal instruction, recitation, study, spiritual practice, and mental attention.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"There are five criteria for the distribution of gains. Which five?"
The gaṇḍī, the triple-staff, the caitya, the wooden tally, and the formal motion constitute the fivefold [set].
Whatever monk arrives when the gaṇḍī for the deceased is being struck, to him the share must be given;
likewise when the triple-staff is being recited, when the veneration of the caitya is being performed, and when the wooden tally is being applied.
Therefore, monks, all the deceased's requisites should be distributed after making a formal motion;
thus it will be irrevocable.
And furthermore, it should be done in this way:

Having prepared the seats and arranged the bedding as previously described, until the entire Saṅgha has sat down and assembled, one should place the requisites for the deceased at the end of the row of elders. Then, a single monk sitting at the end of the row of elders should make the formal motion (jñapti):
"Listen, venerable Saṅgha!"
In this residence, the monk Upananda has passed away;
his personal belongings, both visible and invisible, remain here.

If it seems the proper time to the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, if it so consents, authorize that the Saṃgha shall take formal possession of the deceased monk Upananda’s property, both visible and invisible, as his post-mortem requisites.

This, monks, is the motion (*jñapti*) in this matter; this is the conclusion regarding the distribution of the requisites of the deceased, namely the motion. Once the motion has been made, whatever monk arrives [afterward], no share of the gains is to be given to him.
The Venerable Upāli asked the Buddha, the Blessed One:

"Venerable Sir, in whatever place there is no one who performs the formal motion (*jñapti*) according to the conduct of the Saṃgha, should the requisites of the deceased be distributed there? Or should they not be distributed?"
"Upāli, it should be distributed according to seniority.
But the monks did not know what 'according to seniority' meant.
The Blessed One said:"
Having sold one article of property, a small portion of it should be given to an elder of the Saṃgha and a junior of the Saṃgha, and then the remainder should be distributed as desired;
no remorse should be felt in this matter.
Once the formal motion has been made, whether at the beginning or at the end, the profit from the deceased's belongings accrues to all the disciples of the Buddha.
The monks, having become doubtful, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the dispeller of all doubts:
"Venerable sir, behold how the venerable Upananda has come to ruin through excessive greed.
The Blessed One said:

"Monks, it was not only now that he came to ruin through excessive greed; listen to how it happened in the past as well. Once upon a time, monks, a certain hunter struck an elephant in a vital spot with a poisoned arrow."
Then, struck by that mortal agony, he followed the track of the arrow and killed the hunter.
Just then, by a stroke of fate, about five hundred thieves, having plundered a certain mountain village, arrived at that place;
they saw the elephant.
That time of hardship was occurring;
they said,
"Sirs, this meat is ready."
"Let two hundred and fifty men slaughter the elephant and cook the meat;
let another two hundred and fifty bring water.
Among them, those who slaughtered and cooked—* [MSV II 122] *—[acted as follows].
This thought occurred to them: "Sirs, such a deed has been committed by us,
and this plunder has become abundant."
"Having eaten as much meat as we desire, we shall contaminate the remainder with poison.
Why should we give it to them?
It will become our plunder."
"They will eat the meat tainted with poison and lose their lives.
Having eaten as much meat as they desired, they left the remainder tainted with poison.

Those who were the water-carriers likewise reflected in this same way; having drunk as much water as they desired, they returned without bringing back the remainder, which had been tainted with poison.
Those who ate the meat also drank the water,
and those who drank the water also ate the meat;
all of them passed away.
Meanwhile, a certain jackal, ensnared by the noose of death, arrived at that place;
he saw that they were all dead,
and then, filled with joy through greed, he reflected:
"I have acquired abundant gain;
I must act in due order," he thought,
and he [took up] his bow.
Having placed the bone in his mouth, he began to chew the sinew;
then the sinew was severed, and his palate was pierced by the bone. He passed away.
The deities recited this verse:
"One should indeed practice accumulation, but one should not engage in excessive accumulation;
behold how the jackal, blinded by greed for his hoard, was destroyed."
"What do you think, monks? That jackal at that time and on that occasion was none other than this Upananda.
Even then, he perished through excessive greed;
even now, he has perished through excessive greed."
The setting was Śrāvastī.
At that time, a certain monk was afflicted by illness, suffering, and severely sick; another monk attended to him, yet he nevertheless passed away.
His bowl and robes were brought to the end of the assembly;
there, one robe had been ruined by someone and was swarming with flies.
Then the distributor of robes said to that attendant,
"Venerable one, you are lazy;
you have not even washed this robe."
"Make them grieve!
He replied,
"You shall divide the requisites."
"I shall cause [him] to grieve; you yourself must grieve.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Six requisites should be given to the attendant of the sick person;
the remainder should be distributed among the monks.
If there are many attendants, all six requisites should be distributed in common among them.
Other monks who were renowned for their great merit passed away;
they possessed many requisites, both the requisites for the ascetic life and the requisites for livelihood,
which had been placed at the end of the seniority row.
The Blessed One said,
"An attendant should take six requisites.
Having reflected upon this again and again, he takes those that are excellent.
The Blessed One said,
"Exquisite things should not be given.
The monks gave coarse things.
The Blessed One said:
"Coarse [robes] should not be given; rather, middling ones should be given."
The sick die quite unexpectedly upon the bedding and seats belonging to the Saṅgha.
The Blessed One said:
"The attendant of the sick must be skilled in the signs of the sick; he must examine them repeatedly and must not neglect any duty."
"Having ascertained the state of his body, he should be brought under some pretext onto a bed or seat belonging to a layperson and laid down there.
The setting was Śrāvastī.
A certain monk fell ill; having diagnosed the state of his body, he spoke to another monk:
"As long as I live, perform service for me;
after I have died, my bowl and robes shall be yours as you please.
He then began to provide him with service.
When that monk had passed away,
the distributor of robes said to him,
"Bring the bowl and robes of that monk."
"I am distributing it.
He replied, "He has done as he pleased with that very thing; let it be mine alone."
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said,
"Monks, that man does not give even while he is still alive."
How much less, then, will one who is dead give?
[Thinking: "This gift of mine does not exist after my passing; it shall belong to him," one should take it and distribute it.
"In this matter, monks, a fair portion must be given to him.
Now at that time, a certain monk was afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill;
moreover, he was little known.
There was no medicine for him;
having assessed the state of his body, he said to his attendant,
"I have nothing."
"Perform a worship ceremony dedicated to me," he said;
the other consented,
and then he passed away.
He was reborn in the states of woe.
Then the Blessed One addressed the monks:
"Monks, what did that deceased monk say to his attendant?"
They related the events exactly as they had occurred:
"O monks, that monk has fallen into ruin.
Had his fellow practitioners performed worship of the Three Jewels on his behalf, his mind would have become serene."
Therefore, a monk must not neglect a fellow practitioner who is ill.
An attendant for the sick should be assigned;
if he has no medicine, [the monk] should ask him [for it].
The donors should be encouraged [to provide the requisites].
If they are obtained, that is well;
if they are not obtained, those belonging to the Saṃgha should be given.
If it is obtained, that is well.
If it is not obtained, it should be given from the inexhaustible treasury of the Buddha.
If that also is not obtained, then whatever is to be given by the Saṅgha—whether an umbrella, a banner, a flag, or an ornament—at a Tathāgata’s shrine or in the fragrant chamber, should be given.
The attendant should provide service after having sold [the item], and perform worship for the Teacher.
Once the patient has recovered, it should be reported to him: "That which belonged to the Buddha and was used by you is yours.
This is provided that he has the means to do so.
Therefore, making an effort, he should give [it];
even if that which was used by him is not present,
the son is entitled to his father's property.
"No regret should be felt in this matter.
The setting was Śrāvastī.
A certain monk was afflicted, suffering, gravely ill, and overwhelmed by painful sensations.
His alms-bowl was beautiful;
he was exceedingly attached to it and said to his attendant:
"Bring me my bowl," he said. He did not give it.
Having conceived a malicious thought toward him and being attached to that bowl, he passed away.
In that very bowl, he was reborn as a venomous serpent.
The monks, having carried him to the cremation ground and performed the funeral rites, returned to the monastery;
the community of monks then assembled.
The robe-distributor placed the deceased's personal effects at the head of the assembly of elders.
Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
Go, Ānanda,
and announce to the monks:
"No one at all shall release the bowl-cloth of that monk."
"The Tathāgata himself will release him.
The Venerable Ānanda informed the monks,
and then the Blessed One released him by his own power.
The venomous serpent remained there with its hood expanded;
then the Blessed One, having awakened it with the sound of a snap of his fingers, said:
"Go, you deluded man!"
"Discard this vessel;
let the monks divide it among themselves.
Enraged, he entered the dense forest, wandering at his own will.
Blazing with the fire of anger,
he set that dense forest on fire;
being consumed right there, and having developed a deeply corrupted mind toward the monks, he was reborn in the hells.
Thereupon the Blessed One addressed the monks:
"Monks, you should become disenchanted with all states of existence;
you should become disenchanted with all causes for rebirth into existence—in which, indeed, the body of a single being is burned in three places."
In the dense forest by the fire of anger;
in hell by the hellish one;
in the cremation ground by the ordinary one.

Therefore, a monk should not give rise to excessive attachment toward his requisites; whatever such attachment arises toward, that must be relinquished. If he does not relinquish it, [he commits an offense].
One incurs an offense of transgression;
however, if one who is ill asks for his own requisites,
the attendant must give them to him very quickly.
If one does not give it, one incurs an offense of transgression. The setting was in Śrāvastī.
Now at that time, a certain monk who was ill passed away in his cell and was reborn among non-human beings.
A monk who was the distributor of robes began to enter that cell.
Thinking, "I shall distribute the bowl and robe," he rose up with intense agitation, took a club, and said,
"Lead me away! (MSV II 127)
"Divide the bowls and robes for now," he said;
terrified, he fled.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"First, the deceased monk must be carried out; afterwards, his bowl and robes are to be distributed.
The setting was Śrāvastī.
Now at that time, a certain monk had passed away.
The monks, having carried him out and discarded him in the cemetery in this very manner, returned to the monastery.
The distributor of robes entered his cell.
Thinking, "I shall divide the bowl and robes," he was reborn among non-human beings;
taking up a club, he rose up.
He said,
"As long as you perform the worship of my body, so long do you divide the bowl and robes.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"The monks must first perform the worship of his body;
only after that should the bowl and robes be distributed."
Thinking, "This disadvantage shall not occur," the setting was Śrāvastī.
At that time, a certain monk who was ill passed away in his cell.
That monk, having been taken to the cremation ground and performed with funeral honors, was burned;
he then returned to the monastery,
where the robe-distributor entered his cell.
Taking up a staff, he rose up and said, "In the meantime, grant me a teaching on the Dharma; meanwhile, divide the robes.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Having provided a hearing of the Dharma for his sake and having dedicated the gift, the robes should subsequently be distributed.
The summary verse (uddāna) is as follows:
Then the sick man and the guild-president, acting as overseers of the new construction,
established a boundary and had eight [pillars] set up by means of a messenger.
The setting was in Śrāvastī.
Now at that time, a certain householder invited the community of monks, headed by the Buddha, for a meal at his home;
the community of monks entered.
The Blessed One remained with the alms-food he had received, staying in a place where there was no further accumulation of material goods.
For five reasons, the Buddha-Blessed Ones remain in such places, having accepted their alms-food.
What are these five?
They become desirous of seclusion;
they become desirous of teaching the Dharma to the deities;
they become desirous of inspecting their lodgings.
He wished to visit the sick,

and he wished to prescribe the rules of training for the discipline of the disciples; however, on this occasion, for two reasons, the Buddha, the Blessed One, remained behind with regard to material things, having already finished his alms-round.
Then the Blessed One, perceiving that the community of monks had not long departed, took his key and walked about, traversing monastery after monastery, cell after cell, and walkway after walkway.
While he was thus wandering and moving about,
he approached a certain large dwelling.
There, a monk who was severely ill and lacked attendants, submerged in his own urine and excrement, let out a cry upon seeing the Blessed One:
"I am without a protector, Blessed One! I am without a protector, Sugata!"
The Blessed One said:
"Why, O monk, having gone forth under me, the Lord of the Three Worlds, do you cry out thus?
'I am without a protector, Blessed One!'"
“I am without a protector, O Sugata. Venerable Sir, no fellow-practitioner attends to me or looks after me.
“Bhikṣu, is there anyone to whom you belong? (MSV II 129)
"Did you attend upon or look after your fellow practitioners?
"No, Venerable Sir.
"It is for this very reason that you have come to this state."
The Blessed One gave rise to a worldly thought:
"O, would that Śakra, Lord of the Devas, were to take water from the great lake Anavatapta and bring earth from Mount Gandhamādana!
Indeed, it is the nature of things that whenever the Blessed One gives rise to a worldly thought, at that very moment the gods, including Śakra and Brahmā, understand the Blessed One’s thought.
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, took a golden pitcher of water endowed with the eight qualities from the great lake Anavatapta, and very quickly taking earth from Mount Gandhamādana,
stood before the Blessed One and spoke thus:
"Let the Blessed One remain; I shall attend upon him.
The Blessed One said, "Kauśika, he did not go forth for my sake, but rather for mine."
But why was this not seen by you before?
Stay here;
the gods desire purity.

"I myself shall attend to him. Then the Blessed One, having adjusted his robe, took hold of that monk with his hand— which was marked with the wheel, the svastika, and the nandyāvarta, produced from hundreds of merits, and capable of providing comfort to the frightened— and having lifted him out of the urine and excrement,
he placed him in a secluded spot.
He was scraped with a bamboo splinter,
rubbed with pale clay, bathed,
and then set down.
His robes were washed;
in that place, a smooth coating of cow dung was applied.
Then, having thoroughly cleansed his hands and feet, he attended upon Śakra, the lord of the gods, beginning with the nursing of the sick.
Having instructed and exhorted them with a teaching on the Dharma, he entered the monastery.
The Venerable Ānanda, having brought back almsfood as a collector of offerings, approached the Blessed One.
It is indeed the nature of things that the Buddha-Blessed Ones greet the monk who brings back the almsfood with this greeting:
"Is the excellent meal finished, and has the community of monks been satisfied?
Thus the Blessed One greeted the Venerable Ānanda.
"Has the excellent meal finished, and has the community of monks been satisfied, Ānanda? he asked.
"It is true, Blessed One;
the excellent food has satisfied the community of monks. Then the Blessed One, taking half of the alms-food, addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
"Go, Ānanda; in that monastery there is a monk who is very ill. Half of the alms-food should be given to him. And when he has eaten it, you should say to him:"
"Venerable sir, you yourself have performed service for the Teacher, and you have shared with him half of your alms-food.
"So be it, Blessed One," the venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One; having taken half of the alms-food and given it to him, he reported everything exactly as he had been instructed.
Then this thought occurred to that monk:
"The Teacher of the Three Worlds has personally attended upon me and given me half of his alms-food.
It would not be fitting for me, having consumed what was given out of faith, to pass my time in indolence."
"What if I were to dwell devoted to the practice of wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night?

Thus, dwelling devoted to the practice of wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night, he perceived this very fivefold wheel of saṃsāra as unstable and wavering, and [he understood] the course of all conditioned phenomena as being subject to falling, decaying, scattering, and destruction.
Having struck down all afflictions through their abandonment, he realized arhatship; he became an arhat,
free from passion for the three realms, regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal, with a mind like space or the palm of a hand, and viewing an axe and sandalwood alike.

"Having split the shell of the egg of ignorance with knowledge, possessing supernormal knowledge through wisdom, having attained the analytical insights, and being turned away from existence, gain, greed, and honor,
he has become one who is worthy of worship, respect, and salutation by the gods including Indra and Upendra.
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the monks:"
"Monks, for these who are ill, there is no mother, no father, nor any other relative; there is none other than you, their fellow practitioners of the holy life.
Therefore, fellow practitioners must attend to one another;
a preceptor must attend to his resident disciple."
By a co-resident toward his preceptor;
by a teacher toward his pupil;
and by a pupil toward his teacher.
A fellow pupil with a fellow pupil;
a fellow teacher with a fellow teacher; a confidant with a confidant.
A companion with a companion;
one who is familiar with another who is familiar;
one who is affectionate toward another who is affectionate.
If one who is isolated from the assembly and possesses little knowledge is ill, the Saṃgha should provide him with an attendant— whether one, two, or many; at the very least,
the entire Saṃgha must provide nursing care.
The monks, having conceived a doubt, questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One, the cutter of all doubts:
"Behold, Venerable Sir, how the Blessed One himself provided such service to that monk, and by him, Arhatship was realized."
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, it is not only now; even in the past, I performed service for him."
And by him the five superknowledges were realized.

Long ago, monks, in a certain hermitage endowed with flowers, fruits, and water, and adorned with various trees, there lived a seer possessed of the five superknowledges. He provided service for a disciple.
He recovered his health; then, he realized the five superknowledges (pañcābhijñā).
What do you think, monks?
He who was the seer at that time and on that occasion was I;
he who was the disciple of that seer was this very monk.
At that time also I performed service for him, and now likewise I have performed service for him.
Again, monks, they asked the Buddha, the Blessed One:
"Venerable Sir, see how the sick man is exceedingly dear to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, it is not only now that those who were very ill were dear to me;
listen to this.
Once upon a time, monks, in the royal capital of Śivaghoṣā, a king named Śibi reigned."
It was prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and crowded with many people.
There was nothing he would not give away to supplicants, especially to the sick.
Eventually, a certain householder who was ill and had been rejected by all the physicians went into the presence of the king.
"Your Majesty, please have medical treatment performed for me.
Thereupon, the king gave an order to the physicians:
"Perform medical treatment for him."
They said,
"Your Majesty, the medicines for this are difficult to obtain. The king said:
"But what kind of medicines are they?
"Your Majesty, one who has never before been angry with anyone since birth—his blood must be used for a gruel to be given for six months;
in this way, his health will be restored."
"It is not otherwise," the king said. "It is true that this medicine is difficult to obtain."
He began to examine his own conduct;
he found that his own conduct was characterized by suffering.
He then began to question his nurse.
“Mother, have I ever been angry with anyone during all this time?
“Prince, when you were on my lap, I myself was never angry with anyone, let alone you. Thereupon, he approached his mother.
She said, "Mother, have I ever been angry with anyone?
"Prince, when you were in my womb, I myself had never been angry with anyone before, let alone you."
He reflected:
"The medicine has been found. Having understood this, he gave an order to the physicians:
"Sirs, I have examined myself."
"I have never before been angry with anyone.
Prick me in the five vital spots.
"Your Majesty, we shall not strike a weapon into Your Majesty's body for the sake of an ordinary man."
The Bodhisattvas were skilled in those various fields of arts and crafts;
the king himself performed the venesection,
and with that blood, he gave him a gruel every day for six months.
He became healthy.
What do you think, monks?
That king at that time and on that occasion was none other than I.
Even then, the sick were dear to me, let alone now.
Again, a wasting disease of the side arose in the prince Śiva;
the king gave an order to the physicians.
"Sirs, perform a medical treatment for this prince.
They replied,
"Your Majesty, let the most excellent ghee be prepared."
Having understood this, all the necessary substances were procured over the course of twelve years;
yet even today, the flesh of the *jīvajīvaka* bird could not be obtained. The physicians then gave orders to the fowlers.
"Come!
Taking a mirror and a cock, go to the seashore.
Having cast down snares there, place the mirror in front of the cock."
The cock, seeing its own reflection, will cry out, "This is a cock!
The curious jīvajīvaka bird, hearing the sound of the cock, will approach it;
this is the means for its capture.
They did exactly as instructed.
Eventually, the living being Jīvajīvaka was caught, bound by the noose of karma;
they took him and set out.
For this is the nature of things: when the world has not long since passed away, even animals become capable of articulating speech.
A jīvajīvaka bird said:
"Sirs, where are you taking me?"
They related exactly what had happened;
he said, "Release me! Release me!"
"Māṃsabala, you speak of medicinal herbs or jewels? They replied, "Show us first; let us see what those medicinal herbs are like."
He replied,
"The strength of my flesh is my bath-water;
take that and go."
Thinking, "These are the jewels," they became suspicious of the king;
setting aside the jewels, they set out taking that very jīvajīvaka bird with them.
In due course, they arrived at the royal capital of Śivaghoṣā. They presented the Jīvajīvaka bird to the king and related the medicinal remedy that had been prescribed by it.
Then the king questioned the jīvajīvaka bird, who replied,
"Your Majesty, my bathing water is the source of my strength."

The king had seven beautiful water-jars filled with excellent water set out. Once he had bathed in them and become thoroughly rested, he assessed his physical strength, leaped up suddenly, and having ascended to the roof of the pavilion, free from fear and terror, he spoke this verse:
First I was a fool, and afterwards these bird-catchers;
then the king and the physicians— this is a complete circle of fools.
Having said this, he departed.
Then the king summoned the physicians and asked them, "Sirs, is this true?"
"Sirs, the bath-water of the jīvajīvaka bird is equal in strength to its flesh.
They replied,
"Your Majesty, it is true."
"Boil the ghee. They boiled the ghee that contained the essence of all things. The prince began to consume it.
Once, in a certain cave of the Himalayas where five hundred pratyekabuddhas resided, one among them developed a wasting disease of the flanks.
He was addressed by those pratyekabuddhas:
"Venerable sir, go to the inhabited regions, consult a physician, and take medicine."
"You will become well," he said. "Venerable ones, they will arrive."

"That phenomenon—namely, what is called death—is disliked by many people, unloved by many people, unpleasant to many people, disagreeable to many people, and it is the common lot of all sentient beings; that which will carry me away with disease—for whose sake, then, should I go to the outskirts of the village?
They replied:
"Venerable one, even if it be so, nevertheless, as long as a virtuous person lives, he produces much merit;
and as long as he produces much merit, for that long he rejoices in the heavens.
Being obstructed by those [demons], he descended from the countryside."
In due course, he arrived at the capital city of Śivaghoṣā;
then, having dispelled the fatigue of the journey, he went into the presence of a physician and said,
"O gentle-faced one, I have such an illness."
"Prescribe a medicine," he said.
He replied,
"Noble sir, this illness of yours is exactly like that of the king's son."
"Go and request [it from him]; he has cooked ghee, the essence of all things, for twelve years.
Even if he gives you only the scum of it," [he said].
"By a special stroke of fortune you have been found; therefore, your journey shall be accomplished.
He went and stood at the gate of the royal palace.
It was the custom of that king:
A bell was constantly suspended at the gate to announce the arrival of beggars;
whenever a beggar stood at the gate, it would ring.
When that bell began to ring, announcing that a Pratyekabuddha had arrived,
the prince said,
"Mother, Father, someone has come."
"Consider what it is he requests.
The two of them said,
"Son, after we twelve had gathered wealth over twelve years, this ghee was prepared."

"Drink first; afterwards we shall let the beggar enter and consider what he requests. To him, who had performed the auspicious rites for success and desired to drink the ghee, but whose body was struck at its vital point by the hope placed in the beggar's vessel, that proposal did not please.
And he said,
"Mother, Father, I will not eat until the beggar has entered.
The king gave an order to the doorkeeper.
"Bring in the beggar. He was brought in and seen by the prince.
He was pleasing in body and pleasing in mind, having entered with a tranquil deportment;
he asked,
"What is the purpose of my grandfather?"
He related it in detail. He said,
"Noble one, you alone are worthy of the *maṇḍa*, not I."
"Take it; I give it.
He then extended his bowl.
With intense resolve, the prince gave that broth to him;
and by that noble being, a mind was generated that is devoted to the welfare of all sentient beings.
The mental aspiration of one who possesses ethical discipline succeeds, and that is because of the purity of his ethical discipline; thus,
both became healthy once again.
"What do you think, monks? That prince at that time and on that occasion was none other than myself.
Even then, the sick were dear to me; how much more so now!"
"Venerable Sir, what karma was performed by that prince and by that pratyekabuddha, such that a disease arose for both of them simultaneously and was simultaneously pacified?
The Blessed One said:

"Monks, in previous births in that very same life, those karmas were performed and accumulated; their conditions have been gathered, their causes have matured, they have arrived like a flood, and their result is inevitable."
Monks, actions performed and accumulated do not ripen in the external earth element, nor in the water element,
nor in the fire element.

Nor do they ripen in the wind element; rather, it is within the earth elements themselves—within the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases—that the actions performed, whether wholesome or unwholesome, reach their fruition.
Actions do not perish, even after hundreds of eons.
Having obtained the necessary conditions and the right time, the actions of embodied beings indeed bear fruit.
Once upon a time, monks, there was a king named Brahmadatta in the city of Vārāṇasī.
He had two sons;
of these two, the younger one was a seeker of the kingdom.
The family priest also had two sons;
of these two, the younger one aspired to the office of priest.
Since beings are drawn together by their constituent elements, a mutual friendship arose between them.
The prince said,
"What means might there be by which I could become king?
He replied:
"There is a means:
if you appoint me to the office of domestic chaplain,
I shall tell you."
He said,
"So be it; speak."
"I shall establish it," he said;
the other replied,
"I shall make your brother crippled."
"You shall become king," he said;
and he gave his consent.
Then, he gave medicine to that eldest prince.
He became deformed.
At a later time, the king passed away;
because he was deformed, the ministers consecrated the younger son in the kingdom.
He, in turn, established that younger son of the family priest in the office of domestic chaplain.
Later, on another occasion, while the king was engaged in conversation with the family priest,
he saw his brother who was maimed.
Upon seeing that, remorse arose in him:
"I have done what is not good, in that for the sake of a kingdom I have maimed my brother.
The domestic priest said:
"Your Majesty, a doubt has also arisen within me;
if it pleases Your Majesty, I shall once again restore everything to its former state.
He replied:
"Do so; I give you my permission. He gave him the medicine, and he was restored to health.
Then, having performed services for the Pratyekabuddha, the two of them began to make a formal vow:

"By the ripening of this karma of having performed services for such a truly worthy recipient of offerings, may we both be born into a family that is wealthy, possessing great riches and great enjoyments;
yet, may I experience the ripening of this sinful deed of causing him to become physically deformed."
"What do you think, monks?
That prince at that time, on that occasion, was none other than myself.
That son of the family priest was this very Pratyekabuddha."
Because they administered medicine to the prince after conversing with one another, he became disabled in both limbs simultaneously;
but because they administered medicine again after reflecting with remorse, he was restored to health simultaneously.
Thus, monks, for actions that are entirely black, the ripening is entirely black.
For those that are exclusively white, the result is exclusively white;
for those that are mixed, the result is mixed.
Therefore, monks, having abandoned actions that are exclusively black and those that are mixed, you should apply yourselves only to actions that are exclusively white.
"Thus, monks, you should train yourselves.
The setting was Śrāvastī.

Now at that time, in Śrāvastī, there was a householder named Śreṣṭhin, who was wealthy, possessed of great riches and great enjoyments, with extensive and vast holdings, equal in wealth to Vaiśravaṇa, and rivaling the wealth of Vaiśravaṇa.
He brought home a wife from a family of equal status.
Being childless and longing for a son, he made supplications to Śiva, Varuṇa, Kubera, Śakra, Brahmā, and other distinguished deities;

that is to say, he supplicated the deities of gardens, the deities of groves, the deities of crossroads, the deities of junctions, the deities who receive offerings, as well as innate deities, deities associated with his dharma, and even those deities who are constantly attached to him.
There is this worldly proverb:
"Sons and daughters are born because of prayers";
but that is not so.
If it were so, each person would have a thousand sons, just like a universal monarch (cakravartin). Rather, sons and daughters are born through the coming together of three conditions.
What are these three?
The mother and father are filled with passion and come together;
the mother is healthy and in her fertile season.
And a gandharva becomes present;
through the manifestation of these three conditions, sons and daughters are born.
When, despite propitiating the deities, he had neither son nor daughter, he then rejected all other gods and placed his faith in the Blessed One.
He approached a certain monk and said,
"Noble one, I wish to go forth in the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya."
"Good sir, do so.
Having thus gradually performed the shaving of his hair for him, he began to have him undertake the precepts;
however, [the youth] was overcome by a severe fever that acted as an obstacle to his going forth.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"His attendance must be performed."
"The training rules (śikṣāpada) are not to be conferred as long as he has not recovered," so said the Blessed One.
"His attendance must be performed," yet the monks did not know by whom it was to be performed.
The Blessed One said: "O monks,
physicians administer medicine to him during the day."
At night his illness increased.
They said,
"Noble one, we provide medical treatment for him during the day, yet at night his illness increases."
"If he is taken home, we shall perform medical treatment for him at night.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One,
and the Blessed One said:
"Let him be taken home, and there provide him with attendants.
His illness became chronic,
and his hair grew very long indeed.
He became known by the name Muṇḍa the Householder.
When he did not recover despite being attended with medicines consisting of roots, stalks, leaves, flowers, and fruits, he then realized his own condition, thinking, "I am dead.
Thereupon, at the time of his death, he had all his personal property recorded in writing and sent it to Jetavana.
He passed away.
The ministers informed King Prasenajit of Kosala:
"Your Majesty, the householder Muṇḍa has died without a son."
He possessed abundant gold and bullion, as well as elephants, horses, cattle, buffaloes, and armor;
and having committed all of this to writing on a document, it was sent to the Noble Saṅgha at the Jeta Grove.
The king said:
"I have not even received what was written on a leaf belonging to the noble Upananda, let alone what was written on a formal document;
however, I shall accept whatever the Blessed One permits."
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Monks, what was found there?"
The intermediate summary verse:
The subject matter, bedding, seating, and clothing; iron and copper, and sandalwood; jars, yellow food and so forth, dyeing, the staff, and the jackal.
Whether it be bipeds or quadrupeds, up to food, drink, and medicine,
or even a slave, a bed, or a written document, one should distribute them according to what is appropriate.
"Gold, fine gold, and whatever else is wrought or unwrought, the entire Saṃgha should distribute; so it was declared by the Great Sage."
The monks reported this,
and the Blessed One said:
"It should be distributed according to what is appropriate."
In that regard, the property of fields consists of: the site of a house, the site of a shop;
bedding and seating; the implements of a blacksmith, the implements of a metalworker, and the implements of a potter;
as well as the tools of a carpenter and the tools of a weaver, excluding water-pots and baskets.
The food and drink for female and male slaves, laborers, and servants, as well as the rice, are not to be divided;
they should be set aside as common property for the Saṅgha of monks from the four directions.
Likewise, cotton cloths, woven garments, leather vessels, sandals, oil-jars, water-pots, and water-flasks [are not to be divided].
And they are to be distributed by the entire Saṃgha.
Those staffs that are long are to be made into flagstaffs for the image under the Jambū tree;
those that are short are to be made into *khaṃkharaka* (small sticks) and given to the monks.
Sons and wives should not be sold by the Saṅgha at will; they should be released using whatever has been obtained through [the donor’s] faith.
Among four-footed animals, elephants, horses, camels, donkeys, and mules are for the use of the king;
buffaloes, goats, and sheep are for the Saṅgha of monks from the four directions.
The common items are indivisible;
whatever armor there is, and whatever else is suitable for the king's use, all that must be presented to the king.
Setting aside the weapons, they should have needles and small tools made from those blades and distribute them among the Saṃgha.
The primary pigments—such as yellow orpiment, vermilion, royal blue, and so forth—which are suitable for use on images, should be deposited in the fragrant chamber (gandhakuṭī).
Chalk, white chalk, and indigo should be distributed by the Saṃgha.
As for wine, one should bury it in the ground after mixing it with sweet barley.

When it has turned sour, it may be consumed; however, if it is not fit for use because it is sour, it should be discarded. Monks, those who designate me as their Teacher must not give liquor nor drink it, even to the extent of a drop on the tip of a blade of kusha grass.
Medicines should be placed in the infirmary;
from there, they are to be consumed by the sick monks.
Among jewels, excluding pearls, but including gems, lapis lazuli, and right-spiraling conch shells, two portions must be made:
one for the Dharma and the second for the Saṃgha.
That which belongs to the Dharma should be caused to be written out as the word of the Buddha and used for a lion throne;
that which belongs to the Saṃgha should be distributed by the monks.

Among books, those containing the word of the Buddha (buddhavacana) should be placed in a storage chest for the sake of the Saṅgha of monks from the four directions, without being divided. Books of non-Buddhist treatises (bahiḥśāstra) should be sold by the monks and the proceeds distributed.
As for documents on leaf-paper that can be quickly finalized, those monks should distribute the value of such items.
It is not possible to maintain that for the Saṃgha of monks from the four directions;
it should be deposited in a storehouse.
Gold, silver, and other items, whether worked or unworked, shall be divided into three portions.
The first is for the Buddha; the second is for the Dharma; the third is for the Saṃgha.
That which belongs to the Buddha must be used to repair any broken or dilapidated parts of the fragrant chamber (*gandhakuṭī*) and the reliquaries for hair and nails (*keśanakhastūpa*).
That which belongs to the Dharma must be used to have the word of the Buddha transcribed, or it may be used for a lion throne (*siṃhāsana*).
That which belongs to the Saṅgha must be distributed among the monks.
The setting was Śrāvastī.
When King Prasenajit of Kosala had established the Toyikā festival, there occurred a great assembly of monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen.
At that time, there was a monk named Mūlaphalguna who was to be ordained as a nun.
When the Toyikā festival had arrived, he was addressed by many bhikṣuṇīs:
"Noble sir, please accept our invitation; we shall go to the Toyikā festival."
He said, "Who will place my bowl and robe here?
The group of twelve bhikṣuṇīs replied: [They did so].
"Noble one, do not worry;
we shall set it aside.
He then entrusted it to them.
That was entrusted by them to Mahāprajāpatī;
Mahāprajāpatī entrusted it to the Venerable Ānanda;
and the Venerable Ānanda deposited it in a certain monastery.
Then the Venerable Mūlaphalguna went to the festival at Toyikā.
There he was invited by the bhikṣuṇīs; one of them said:
"The Noble One must perform his morning duties today.
He was invited for the morning session,
and again for the afternoon session.
Another said,
"The Noble One should eat from my presence," and yet another said the same.
In this very way another also speaks; yet another says,
"The Noble One must have me drink a time-drink."
Another spoke in the same way, and yet another spoke likewise;
therefore, out of consideration for them, he took only small amounts at a time and made his morning meal.
At that very time, food was eaten and a drink was drunk at an improper hour;
then, little by little, it became abundant.
He was exhausted from the journey,
and he ate a great deal; consequently,
he became indigestible.
Viṣūcita passed away;
the monks carried him to the cremation ground, cremated him,
and offered a discourse on the Dharma.
Having entered the monastery in due order,
he was addressed by the robe-keeper:
"Bring his bowl and robes."
He said,
"It was placed in the hands of the group of twelve.
They were questioned.
They said,
"We placed it in the hands of Mahāprajāpatī. Mahāprajāpatī said:
"I have entrusted it to Ānanda," [he said].
The venerable Ānanda replied,
"I have deposited it in that monastery."
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Ānanda, a monk must formally designate each individual item as belonging to the estate of the deceased."
And furthermore, it should be performed in this manner:

having prepared the seating and bedding, struck the gong, and questioned the monks by means of a formal inquiry, when the entire Saṃgha has sat down and assembled, one monk should make a motion (*jñapti*) and the ritual act (*karman*) should be carried out.
"Let the venerable Saṃgha listen. In this residence, the monk Mūlaphalguna has passed away.
His bowl and robes, together with the robe-fund, are held in the hands of Ānanda."
"If it seems timely to the Saṅgha, may the Saṅgha grant its permission:
that the Saṅgha should authorize the bowl and robes, along with the robe-fund, of the monk Mūlaphalguna as the estate of the deceased, to be administered by the monk Ānanda. This was the motion.
The Venerable Upāli questioned the Buddha, the Blessed One.
"Venerable sir, if a monk should pass away elsewhere, and his bowl and robes are elsewhere, while his residence is elsewhere—
to whom does that bowl and robe belong? Upāli, it belongs to whichever monk or householder is the resident there."
The setting was Śrāvastī.
At that time, a monk who had been in charge of construction work passed away.
Out of remorse, the monks did not distribute his bowl and robes.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Having assembled the entire Saṅgha, he is to be examined."
Is he one who acts with confusion or not?
If he acts with confusion,
he treats what belongs to the Saṅgha as if it belonged to a stūpa.
Whether it be property belonging to a stūpa or property belonging to the Saṅgha,
such is unrighteous.
His bowl and robes, along with the cloth for the robes, must be divided into three portions.
Of the Buddha, of the Dharma, and of the Saṅgha.
That which belongs to the Saṅgha is to be distributed among the monks.

With that which belongs to the Buddha, worship of the Buddha should be performed, or new construction work should be carried out on a perfumed chamber or a stūpa. With that which belongs to the Dharma, the word of the Buddha should be committed to writing.
Or it may be used for a lion-throne;
if it is not a composite object, it must be divided among all the monks.
No remorse should be felt in this matter.
The setting was Śrāvastī.
At that time, a great number of monks, wandering on a journey through the countryside, arrived in succession at Śrāvastī, near the city.
Among them, one monk passed away.
They reflected:
"Let us divide [the goods] outside the monastery;
for once we have entered the monastery, our fellow celibates will also demand a share."
Śrāvastī was crowded on all sides by cowherds, shepherds, grass-gatherers, wood-gatherers, and people who lived by the paths or by wandering off the paths.
Wherever they sat down, thinking, "Let us divide [the food]," they were surrounded by a great multitude of people.
They reflected:
"Let us divide [the goods] near the monastery.
They began to divide them near the monastery. They were seen by the superintendent of the monastery's requisites and addressed by him:
"Venerable ones, what are you doing?
They related exactly what had occurred,
and he said:
"I too have reached the boundary. Even as he disputed with them in this way, they did not give it to him. The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"If those who perceive themselves as being within the boundary divide the requisites of the deceased while they are indeed within the boundary, it is not divided;
it is wrongly divided."
Furthermore, they must share [the property] together with those who have reached the boundary;
otherwise, they commit an offense of transgression.
Thus, those within the boundary who are in doubt share [the property].
What has not been distributed is improperly distributed; it must be redistributed together with those who have reached the boundary. Otherwise, they commit an offense of transgression.

If those who perceive it as being within the boundary divide the requisites of the deceased while they are outside the boundary, that division is not made; it is an improper division. They must divide them again together with those who have reached the boundary.
Otherwise, they commit an offense of transgression. If they divide [the property] outside the boundary while being in doubt, it is not divided; it is improperly divided.
Furthermore, they must share [the gains] together with those who have reached the boundary;
otherwise, they become guilty of an offense.
The setting was Śrāvastī.
At that time, a monk sent robes for another monk by means of a third monk's hand.
That [third] monk consumed them by means of a sigh from the one to whom they were sent.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"O monks, that monk produced trust where there was no trust.
By whichever monk those [items] were sent, they were consumed by him with that same trust."
Moreover, a monk sends robes for a monk into the hand of another monk;
he uses them with trust in the one to whom they were sent,
and they are used well.
One partakes of those [offerings] by means of the breath of the one who sent them;
they are difficult to consume. // 1 //
A monk sends robes to another monk;
the one to whom they were sent has died, as has the one by whom they were sent. (MSV II 148)
He enjoys those things out of trust,
yet they are improperly enjoyed;
he appropriates them as the deceased's personal effects according to the rule for the one to whom they were sent.
They are well-established. // 2 //
A monk sends robes to another monk;
the one to whom they were sent has died.
The one by whom they were sent, according to the rule, consecrates them as the deceased's personal effects.
Ill-directed. // 3 //
A monk sends robes to another monk;
they are rejected by the one to whom they were sent,
yet the sender uses them with confidence, trusting that they belong to him.
They are well-enjoyed;
he enjoys them with confidence because they were sent by someone in whom he trusts.
They are not poorly enjoyed. // 4 //
A monk sends robes to another monk;
the one to whom they were sent has passed away.
The one to whom they were sent designates them as the estate of the deceased according to the rule.

They are well-consecrated when one consecrates them as requisites for the deceased according to the ritual procedure of the person by whom they were sent; otherwise, they are poorly consecrated. // 5 //
A monk sends robes to another monk;
they are rejected by the one to whom they were sent,
and the one who sent them has passed away.
One consumes with trust that which has been sent by another;
thus it is improperly consumed.
One designates as an article for the deceased that which was sent by someone else according to their own calculation.
Well-established. // 6 //
A monk sends robes to another monk;
they are rejected by the one to whom they were sent,
and he passes away.
He by whom they were sent has passed away;
he for whose sake they were sent consecrates them as requisites for the deceased according to the ritual procedure.
They are ill-consecrated.
He consecrates those items as requisites for the deceased according to the ritual procedure by which they were sent; thus they are well-consecrated. // 7 //
The section on robes is completed.
